shard.title: West and Central Africa
shard.author: regional historian: West and Central Africa
shard.note: British West Africa from the Gold Coast forts of the 1630s to Nigeria in 1960 and the British Cameroons in 1961. Only 16 geo units exist for this region, so several sub-degree possessions (Cape Coast Castle, Elmina, the Danish forts, Fort James, Bunce Island, MacCarthy Island, Ambas Bay, Gorée) are recorded as point-scale territories that hatch a whole unit and carry the gap in the coverage 'change' field. Where two forts sit inside one unit the validator reports geo/overlapping-claim; those warnings are expected and correct.

territories.name: Province of Senegambia
territories.formalName: The Province of Senegambia

namesOverTime.name: Ndar
namesOverTime.note: The Wolof name for the island the French called Saint-Louis, and still the everyday name for the town.

modernSuccessors.name: Senegal
modernSuccessors.note: Independent from France, not from Britain. Saint-Louis was French again from 1783 and stayed French for 177 years.

geoCoverage.label: Saint-Louis and the Senegal river trade
geoCoverage.change: A British squadron took the French fort at Saint-Louis; Britain held the river mouth and the gum trade, not the interior.

geoCoverage.label: Saint-Louis plus the Gambia forts
geoCoverage.change: The Crown joined the Gambia forts to Saint-Louis under one governor and called the whole thing the Province of Senegambia.

acquisitions.how: A squadron sent on the urging of Thomas Cumming, a Quaker merchant who wanted the gum trade, sailed up the Senegal bar and forced the French garrison at Saint-Louis to capitulate.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: France lost Saint-Louis, its oldest African settlement, and with it the monopoly on Senegal river gum arabic that Bordeaux merchants depended on.

counterparties.name: The Waalo kingdom and the Trarza emirate
counterparties.lost: They lost nothing in law and a great deal in practice: the customs payments, presents and trade terms they had negotiated with the French had to be renegotiated with a new set of foreigners who arrived with warships.

people.name: Thomas Cumming
people.role: Quaker merchant who lobbied William Pitt for the expedition and sailed with it

people.name: Henry Marsh
people.role: commanded the naval force that took Saint-Louis

acquisitions.resistance: The French garrison of about 230 men surrendered after a short bombardment; the Wolof and Moorish traders on the river simply carried on selling gum to whoever held the fort.

contested.note: Accounts differ on the exact day of the capitulation and on the size of the garrison. The month is secure.

evidence.author: Philip D. Curtin
evidence.work: Economic Change in Precolonial Africa: Senegambia in the Era of the Slave Trade
evidence.supports: The gum trade, the river economy and the European posts on it.

acquisitions.how: Parliament stripped the Company of Merchants Trading to Africa of its Gambia forts and put them, with Saint-Louis, under a Crown governor at Saint-Louis: the first British Crown colony anywhere in Africa.

counterparties.name: Company of Merchants Trading to Africa
counterparties.lost: The company lost Fort James and its Gambia trade to direct Crown administration, and spent eighteen years lobbying to get them back.

counterparties.name: The kingdom of Niumi
counterparties.lost: Niumi's Mansa had licensed Fort James and taxed its trade since 1661; a Crown government arrived less willing to pay customs to an African ruler than a company had been.

instrument.name: Act for establishing a Crown colony on the coast of Africa (the Senegambia Act)
instrument.note: Contemporary usage varies; the province is dated 1765 by its charter and its first governor arrived in 1766.

people.name: Charles O'Hara
people.role: first governor of Senegambia, 1766-1775; ran the province as a private trading concern and was recalled for it

evidence.author: John D. Hargreaves
evidence.work: Prelude to the Partition of West Africa
evidence.supports: The Senegambia experiment and its collapse.

statusPeriods.label: Military occupation of Saint-Louis
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A naval officer held the fort and licensed the traders; London had no plan for the place beyond denying it to France in wartime.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: the fort at Saint-Louis

statusPeriods.label: Britain's first Crown colony in Africa
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor and council appointed in London ruled a few hundred soldiers and traders on two river mouths and bargained for everything else with the Wolof, Fulbe and Mandinka states around them.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Saint-Louis, under the Secretary of State in London
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. The province had no assembly and its African population had no standing in its courts.
statusPeriods.note: The experiment was judged a failure long before France ended it: the garrison died of fever, the governor traded on his own account, and the Board of Trade could never say what the colony was for.

departures.how: A French force under the duc de Lauzun stormed Saint-Louis in January 1779, and at the Treaty of Versailles in 1783 Britain signed Senegal back to France and kept only the Gambia.

led.name: Armand-Louis de Gontaut, duc de Lauzun
led.role: commanded the French expedition that retook Saint-Louis and Fort James in 1779

led.name: Matthias MacNamara
led.role: British lieutenant-governor whose feuding helped discredit the province before it fell

cost.note: The garrisons surrendered quickly and European losses were counted in dozens. Nobody recorded African deaths in the fighting, which is itself evidence about whose lives the records were kept for.

departures.borders: The 1783 line put France on the Senegal and Britain on the Gambia, and that is why the Gambia today is a 30-kilometre-wide country inside Senegal.

instrument.name: Treaty of Versailles (1783)
instrument.note: The same treaty settlement that recognised the independence of the United States.

evidence.author: John D. Hargreaves
evidence.work: Prelude to the Partition of West Africa
evidence.supports: The dissolution of Senegambia and the retention of the Gambia.

consequences.borderLegacy: Britain kept the river and France kept the country around it, so the Gambia became a 300-kilometre sliver inside Senegal with a border that ignores every language and lineage it crosses.
consequences.economicLegacy: Saint-Louis exported gum arabic for European textile printing and enslaved people for the Americas; the British interlude changed the flags on the warehouses and not the cargoes.

slavery.note: Both flags trafficked people. Saint-Louis and Gorée were assembly points on a coast from which roughly 750,000 people were shipped across the Atlantic between 1500 and 1867.

toll.note: Senegambian embarkation totals come from the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database and are estimates built from surviving ship records; the true figure is higher than the documented one.

evidence.author: John D. Hargreaves
evidence.work: Prelude to the Partition of West Africa
evidence.supports: The Senegambia province, its administration and its cession.

evidence.author: Philip D. Curtin
evidence.work: Economic Change in Precolonial Africa: Senegambia in the Era of the Slave Trade
evidence.supports: The economy of the Senegal and Gambia rivers under European posts.

evidence.author: Donald R. Wright
evidence.work: The World and a Very Small Place in Africa: A History of Globalization in Niumi, The Gambia
evidence.supports: Niumi's relations with Fort James and the customs paid to African rulers.

contested.note: Senegambia is thinly documented and historians differ over whether it was a serious experiment in Crown government or a wartime improvisation nobody in London wanted to pay for.

pedagogy.hook: Britain's first Crown colony in Africa was in Senegal, it lasted eighteen years, and Britain gave it back to France in the same treaty that recognised the United States.

misconception.belief: Britain's African empire began with the Scramble for Africa in the 1880s.
misconception.correction: Britain governed a Crown colony on the Senegal river from 1765, held forts on the Gambia from 1661 and on the Gold Coast from the 1630s, and ran the largest slave-trading operation in the Atlantic from them. The 1880s changed the map; they did not start the story.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows the eighteenth-century pattern: Britain took African coastal posts from other Europeans in European wars, for European reasons, and gave them back in European treaties. The people who lived there were not consulted in 1758, in 1765 or in 1783.

keyDates.what: Britain takes Saint-Louis from France
Province of Senegambia created: the first British Crown colony in Africa
France retakes Saint-Louis
Treaty of Versailles: Senegal to France, the Gambia stays British

territories.name: Gorée Island
territories.formalName: The Island of Gorée

namesOverTime.name: Ber

from.note: A rough marker for the pre-contact period, not an event.

namesOverTime.note: The Lebou name for the island before the Portuguese landed in 1444.

namesOverTime.name: Goede Reede
namesOverTime.note: 'Good roadstead'. The Dutch name survives, francised, as Gorée.

modernSuccessors.name: Senegal
modernSuccessors.note: Gorée is a commune of Dakar and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

geoCoverage.label: The island only, 45 hectares off Cape Verde
geoCoverage.change: Commodore Keppel's squadron took the island from France; no geo unit exists at this scale, so the map draws the whole of Senegal hatched.

geoCoverage.label: British occupation during the Napoleonic Wars
geoCoverage.change: Britain took Gorée again in the wars against Revolutionary and Napoleonic France, lost it briefly at the Peace of Amiens, and held it until the 1814 settlement returned it.

acquisitions.how: Commodore Augustus Keppel's squadron bombarded the two French forts on the island for a few hours until the garrison struck its colours.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: France lost its second Senegal post and, for four years, its share of the Atlantic trade north of the Gambia.

counterparties.name: The Lebou people of the Cape Verde peninsula
counterparties.lost: The Lebou mainland villages that fed and crewed the island kept trading, now with a different European garrison; they had no say in either flag.

people.name: Augustus Keppel
people.role: commodore commanding the squadron that took the island

acquisitions.resistance: The French garrison of roughly 300 surrendered after a short bombardment.

acquisitions.how: British warships took the island back during the war with Revolutionary France; it changed hands again around the Peace of Amiens before Britain reoccupied it for the rest of the war.

counterparties.name: France
counterparties.lost: France lost the island's customs revenue and its use as a privateering base against British West Indiamen.

contested.note: Gorée changed hands so often between 1779 and 1817 that accounts disagree about the exact years of British control; the 1800 recapture and the January 1817 handover are the two fixed points.

evidence.author: John D. Hargreaves
evidence.work: Prelude to the Partition of West Africa
evidence.supports: British and French alternation on the Senegal coast to 1817.

statusPeriods.label: Held by the Royal Navy in the Seven Years' War
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A naval garrison held the forts and licensed the island's trading houses; the signares, the wealthy Afro-European women who owned much of the property, dealt with whichever navy was in the harbour.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: the fort on Gorée, under the naval commander-in-chief

statusPeriods.label: British occupation in the Napoleonic Wars
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A small British garrison held the island; after 1807 it also served the Royal Navy squadron that was now stopping slave ships instead of escorting them.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Gorée, under the governor of Senegal or of Sierra Leone at different dates
statusPeriods.gapReason: The island was French from the Treaty of Paris in February 1763 until the British recapture in 1800. Britain had no authority there in those 37 years, so the record shows a gap rather than a status.
statusPeriods.note: Britain's 1807 abolition of the slave trade turned the same island from a trading post into a base for stopping the trade, without changing the garrison.

departures.how: Under the 1814 peace settlement Britain handed Gorée and Saint-Louis back to France, and French officials resumed control of the island in January 1817.

led.name: Julien-Désiré Schmaltz
led.role: French governor sent to take back Senegal in 1816-17; his expedition included the frigate Méduse, wrecked on the way

cost.note: The handover was administrative and nobody was killed. The French relief expedition itself lost about 150 people when the frigate Méduse ran aground off Mauritania in July 1816 — the wreck Géricault painted.

departures.borders: Gorée going back to France completed the tidy-up of 1783: France on the Senegal coast, Britain on the Gambia and Sierra Leone.

instrument.name: Treaty of Paris (1814)
instrument.note: The handover on the ground took until January 1817.

evidence.author: John D. Hargreaves
evidence.work: Prelude to the Partition of West Africa
evidence.supports: The 1814-17 restoration of Senegal to France.

slavery.note: Gorée was a slave-trading island, and the scale is disputed: careful counts of ship records suggest a few hundred people a year passed through it, not the millions its memorial literature once claimed.

abolitionDate.note: The British Slave Trade Act. France abolished its trade in law in 1815 and in practice much later.

toll.note: Ralph Austen and other historians who compared the Maison des Esclaves tradition with the surviving voyage records concluded that Gorée handled a small fraction of the Senegambian trade. Saying so is not a defence of the trade; it is a warning about how memory sites get their numbers.

consequences.languageAndLaw: Gorée is French-speaking and French-lawed today; the British decades left almost nothing behind except a gap in the customs records.

evidence.author: Ralph A. Austen
evidence.work: The Slave Trade as History and Memory: Confrontations of Slaving Voyage Documents and Communal Traditions
evidence.supports: The gap between Gorée's documented traffic and its remembered scale.

evidence.author: Philip D. Curtin
evidence.work: The Atlantic Slave Trade: A Census
evidence.supports: Regional embarkation estimates for Senegambia.

evidence.author: John D. Hargreaves
evidence.work: Prelude to the Partition of West Africa
evidence.supports: British and French possession of Gorée.

contested.note: Two things are disputed: the exact dates of British occupation between 1779 and 1817, and how many people were shipped from Gorée. On the second, the documentary evidence and the island's oral tradition point to very different orders of magnitude.

pedagogy.hook: Gorée is the world's most visited memorial to the slave trade, and historians who counted the ships think only a small fraction of enslaved Senegambians ever passed through it.

misconception.belief: Millions of enslaved Africans passed through the Door of No Return on Gorée Island.
misconception.correction: The Maison des Esclaves was built around 1776 as a merchant's house, and reconstructions from surviving voyage records suggest Gorée handled hundreds of captives a year, not millions in total. The Atlantic trade was real and vast — roughly 12.5 million people embarked — but it flowed mostly through other ports. A memorial can be true about the crime and wrong about the number.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the cleanest case in this atlas of the difference between memory and evidence. Students who learn to ask 'how was that number produced?' here will ask it of every other figure in the empire.

keyDates.what: Keppel's squadron takes Gorée from France
Treaty of Paris returns Gorée to France
Britain occupies the island again
Gorée handed back to France for good

territories.name: The Gambia
territories.formalName: The Colony and Protectorate of the Gambia

namesOverTime.name: Kambi Bolongo

from.note: A rough marker for the pre-contact period, not an event.

namesOverTime.note: The river's Mandinka name; 'Gambia' is a Portuguese rendering of it. The country is named after the river, which is why it has 'The' in front.

namesOverTime.name: Settlements on the River Gambia
namesOverTime.note: Governed at different times from Saint-Louis, Freetown and London before becoming a colony in its own right in 1888.

namesOverTime.name: Colony and Protectorate of the Gambia

modernSuccessors.name: The Gambia
modernSuccessors.note: A republic since 24 April 1970. It left the Commonwealth in 2013 and rejoined in 2018.

geoCoverage.label: Fort James and the river trade
geoCoverage.change: One fortified island 30 km upriver, licensed by the Mansa of Niumi, who taxed everything that passed it.

geoCoverage.label: Bathurst, MacCarthy Island and the river
geoCoverage.change: The Province of Senegambia was dissolved and the Gambia settlements returned to British company management, then to the Crown in 1821. Britain held river islands and a trading town, not a country.

geoCoverage.label: The Colony and the ten-mile Protectorate strip
geoCoverage.change: The 1889 Anglo-French convention fixed the boundary about ten kilometres from each bank, and the 1894 Protectorate Ordinance brought the riverside chiefdoms under British administration.

acquisitions.how: Captain Robert Holmes seized the small fortified island the Duchy of Courland had built on in 1651 and renamed it James Island after the Duke of York, who ran the English slave-trading company.

counterparties.name: The Duchy of Courland
counterparties.lost: A Baltic duchy lost the only overseas colony it ever had; Courland's African venture ended in a single morning.

counterparties.name: The kingdom of Niumi
counterparties.lost: Niumi lost nothing yet: its Mansa went on licensing the fort and collecting customs on its trade for another 160 years. Sovereignty on the river still belonged to Africans, and everyone involved knew it.

people.name: Robert Holmes
people.role: naval captain who seized the island for the Company of Royal Adventurers Trading into Africa

people.name: James, Duke of York
people.role: governor of the Royal Adventurers and later of the Royal African Company; the island was named for him

acquisitions.resistance: The Courlander garrison was tiny and surrendered. African resistance came later and repeatedly: the fort was besieged, blockaded and starved by neighbouring rulers whenever it stopped paying its customs.

contested.note: The exact day of Holmes's seizure is given differently in different accounts; the month and year are secure.

evidence.author: Donald R. Wright
evidence.work: The World and a Very Small Place in Africa: A History of Globalization in Niumi, The Gambia
evidence.supports: Niumi's licensing of the fort and the customs it collected.

acquisitions.how: Captain Alexander Grant obtained Banjul Island from Tumani Bojang, Mansa of Kombo, for an annual payment in iron bars, and built a town and a battery there to stop slave ships leaving the river.

counterparties.name: The kingdom of Kombo
counterparties.lost: Kombo gave up a sandy island at the river mouth for an annual rent, and got in return a permanent British garrison at the gate of its own kingdom.

instrument.name: Cession of Banjul Island by Tumani Bojang, Mansa of Kombo
instrument.note: The rent was reckoned in iron bars, the river's trade currency. Accounts give the amount as 103 bars a year.

people.name: Alexander Grant
people.role: army captain who founded Bathurst, now Banjul, as an anti-slave-trade base

people.name: Tumani Bojang
people.role: Mansa of Kombo, who ceded the island

evidence.author: Arnold Hughes and David Perfect
evidence.work: A Political History of the Gambia, 1816-1994
evidence.supports: The founding of Bathurst and the growth of the colony.

acquisitions.how: After the 1889 convention with France drew a line about ten kilometres from each bank, Britain declared the chiefdoms inside that line a protectorate and appointed travelling commissioners over them.

counterparties.name: The Mandinka, Fula, Wolof and Jola states of the river
counterparties.lost: Some thirty-five ruling houses lost control of their own foreign relations, their courts' jurisdiction over serious crime, and the right to tax their own people without British sanction.

acquisitions.resistance: The marabout leaders Fodi Silla and Fodi Kabba fought the extension of British power through the 1890s; Fodi Silla was driven into Senegal in 1894 and Fodi Kabba was killed by a joint Anglo-French column in 1901.

evidence.author: Arnold Hughes and David Perfect
evidence.work: A Political History of the Gambia, 1816-1994
evidence.supports: The creation of the Protectorate and the campaigns that followed it.

statusPeriods.label: Company forts licensed by African rulers
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A chartered company held one island and paid customs to the Mansa of Niumi to be allowed to trade; when it stopped paying, the fort was blockaded until it started again.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Fort James, under the Royal African Company in London
statusPeriods.note: The fort was attacked or destroyed by the French in 1695, 1702, 1704, 1708 and 1779, blown up by its own garrison in 1709 and plundered by pirates in 1719. It was a trading post, not a government.

statusPeriods.label: Back under the Company of Merchants
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Company of Merchants Trading to Africa ran the Gambia posts again, on a parliamentary grant, with no fort worth the name after the French destroyed Fort James in 1779.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: the Company of Merchants, London
statusPeriods.gapReason: From 1765 to 1783 the Gambia forts were not a separate British possession: they were governed from Saint-Louis as part of the Province of Senegambia, which has its own record.

statusPeriods.label: Crown settlement at Bathurst
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Parliament abolished the Company of Merchants and vested its forts in the Crown; the Gambia was run from Freetown until 1843, on its own until 1866, from Freetown again until 1888, and then on its own.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Bathurst, under Freetown or the Colonial Office at different dates
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. A governor ruled with a nominated council of officials and merchants.
statusPeriods.note: Between 1866 and 1876 the British government three times proposed swapping the Gambia to France for territory elsewhere. Bathurst's merchants and traders petitioned against it and the deals collapsed.

statusPeriods.label: Colony and Protectorate
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The governor at Bathurst ruled the Colony directly and the Protectorate through head chiefs supervised by two travelling commissioners, who between them administered a country 300 kilometres long.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Bathurst, under the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.franchise: Bathurst got its first elected seat on the Legislative Council in 1947. Protectorate members were chosen by chiefs until 1960, when the whole country voted for the first time.
statusPeriods.note: The Colony and the Protectorate were legally different countries with the same governor: people born in Bathurst were British subjects, people born forty kilometres upriver were British protected persons.

statusPeriods.label: Internal self-government under Jawara
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Dawda Jawara became Prime Minister and Gambian ministers ran everything except defence and foreign affairs for sixteen months.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Bathurst
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage from the 1962 election, the first in which Colony and Protectorate voted on the same roll.

departures.how: After a constitutional conference in London in July 1964, Britain legislated the Gambia into independence and the flag changed at midnight in Bathurst with nobody killed.

led.name: Dawda Kairaba Jawara
led.role: veterinary surgeon, leader of the People's Progressive Party, first Prime Minister and later President

led.name: Pierre Sarr N'Jie
led.role: leader of the United Party and Jawara's main rival, who argued the country was too small to stand alone

led.name: Duncan Sandys
led.role: Secretary of State for the Colonies who chaired the 1964 conference

cost.note: No one died. The Gambia is the counter-example to a violent-decolonisation story: a colony so small and so poor that Britain had nothing to fight for and left when asked.

departures.borders: The border did not move a metre. The Gambia inherited exactly the ten-mile strip France and Britain agreed in 1889, which is why it is a 30-kilometre-wide country wrapped around a river inside Senegal.

instrument.name: Gambia Independence Act 1964
instrument.note: Royal assent December 1964; independence took effect on 18 February 1965.

evidence.author: Arnold Hughes and David Perfect
evidence.work: A Political History of the Gambia, 1816-1994
evidence.supports: The independence negotiations and the 1965 settlement.

slavery.note: For 150 years British ships loaded captives on this river; then for 150 more the same river was policed by British ships stopping the trade. Both were done from the same forts.

emancipationDate.note: The 1833 Act freed people in the Colony. Slavery inside the Protectorate was only abolished by ordinance in 1906, and slave-holding persisted quietly for years afterwards.

toll.note: Estimates for the Gambia river specifically are uncertain; the wider Senegambia region accounts for roughly 750,000 documented embarkations in the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database, of which the Gambia was a substantial share.

consequences.borderLegacy: The Gambia is the smallest country on mainland Africa and one of the strangest shapes on earth, because Britain kept a river and France kept the land on either side of it.
consequences.economicLegacy: Groundnuts became the colony's monocrop in the 1830s and were still about nine tenths of its exports at independence; a country that grew one thing for one market was independent and not economically free.

commonwealth.note: President Yahya Jammeh withdrew the Gambia in 2013, calling the Commonwealth a neo-colonial institution. The country rejoined on 8 February 2018 after he lost power.

consequences.languageAndLaw: English is the official language of a country where most people speak Mandinka, Fula or Wolof, and the courts still run on English common law beside customary and sharia jurisdictions.

peak.populationNote: 1963 census, the last before independence. About 28,000 lived in Bathurst.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: The Gambia’s largest recorded population: 315,486 people, counted in 1963.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Arnold Hughes and David Perfect
evidence.work: A Political History of the Gambia, 1816-1994
evidence.supports: The whole political arc from Bathurst to independence.

evidence.author: Donald R. Wright
evidence.work: The World and a Very Small Place in Africa: A History of Globalization in Niumi, The Gambia
evidence.supports: How the river's African states dealt with European forts over three centuries.

evidence.author: John D. Hargreaves
evidence.work: Prelude to the Partition of West Africa
evidence.supports: The nineteenth-century proposals to exchange the Gambia with France.

pedagogy.hook: Britain three times offered to give the Gambia away to France, and kept it because the traders of Bathurst objected loudly enough.

misconception.belief: Colonial borders were drawn with a ruler across a map by men who had never seen the place.
misconception.correction: Some were. The Gambia's border was surveyed on the ground in 1891 by a joint Anglo-French commission working roughly ten kilometres out from each bank of the river. It is still absurd, and it was still drawn by two European governments with no Gambian in the room. Precision and legitimacy are different things.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Gambia is the empire in miniature: a fort licensed by an African king, a slave trade, an anti-slave-trade squadron using the same buildings, a protectorate over people who were never made subjects, and a peaceful exit that changed nothing about the shape of the map.

keyDates.what: Robert Holmes seizes James Island for the Royal Adventurers
Bathurst founded on Banjul Island as an anti-slave-trade base
Anglo-French convention fixes the Gambia's absurd border
Protectorate declared over the riverside chiefdoms
Independence under Dawda Jawara

territories.name: Fort James (Kunta Kinteh Island)
territories.formalName: James Island and Fort James, River Gambia
territories.subregion: Gambia river, 30 km from the sea

namesOverTime.name: St Andrew's Island
namesOverTime.note: Named by the Duchy of Courland, which built the first fort there in 1651.

namesOverTime.name: James Island
namesOverTime.note: After James, Duke of York, governor of the English slave-trading company.

namesOverTime.name: Kunta Kinteh Island
namesOverTime.note: Renamed by the Gambian government after the character in Alex Haley's Roots, whose family tradition placed his capture on this river.

modernSuccessors.name: The Gambia
modernSuccessors.note: A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2003, and eroding: the island is a fraction of its seventeenth-century size.

geoCoverage.label: One island of a few hectares, 30 km upriver
geoCoverage.change: No geo unit exists at this scale, so the map hatches the whole of the Gambia and marks the island with a point.

acquisitions.how: Robert Holmes took the Courlanders' fort, renamed it after the Duke of York, and turned it into the collecting point where captives from the upper river were held until a ship came.

counterparties.name: The Duchy of Courland
counterparties.lost: Courland lost the fort it had built in 1651 and with it any share in the Atlantic trade.

counterparties.name: The kingdom of Niumi
counterparties.lost: Niumi kept its sovereignty and its customs revenue for another century and a half, and lost the ability to keep any single European power out.

people.name: Robert Holmes
people.role: seized the island in March 1661

contested.note: The exact day of the seizure varies between accounts; the month is agreed.

statusPeriods.label: Slave fort of the Royal African Company
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A company agent held the island with a few dozen soldiers, most of whom died of fever, and bought captives from Mandinka, Fula and Serahuli traders who brought them down the river.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: the Royal African Company, then the Company of Merchants, in London
statusPeriods.note: The fort was taken or destroyed by the French in 1695, 1702, 1704, 1708 and 1779, blown up by its own garrison in 1709, and sacked by the pirate Howell Davis in 1719. After 1779 it was never rebuilt.

statusPeriods.label: A Crown ruin
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The island passed to the Crown with the rest of the Company of Merchants' property and was governed from Bathurst as an uninhabited historic site; nothing was administered there because nobody lived there.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Bathurst

departures.how: The island passed to the independent Gambia with the rest of the country, and the state that inherited it later renamed it after a fictional captive who stood for the real ones.

led.name: Dawda Kairaba Jawara
led.role: led the Gambia to independence

cost.note: Nobody died in 1965. The deaths that belong to this island happened between 1661 and 1807 and were never counted.

departures.borders: The island's status did not change at independence; it changed its name in 2011, which mattered more to how Gambians tell the story.

slavery.note: Fort James was a holding pen: captives taken in wars and raids far up the Gambia were kept in its cells until a slave ship anchored, then rowed out to it.

statusPeriods.label: The Province of Freedom: no charter, no Crown
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The settlers elected their own tithingmen and hundredors under a constitution Granville Sharp wrote for them, on land a Temne ruler had licensed. Britain claimed no sovereignty and sent no governor.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: the settlers' own elected officers, advised by a committee in London
statusPeriods.franchise: Every settler household head, male and female, could vote in the settlement's own courts and elections — a franchise wider than anything in Britain at the time, in a place Britain did not govern.
statusPeriods.note: This is the only status in the whole atlas where colonists governed themselves more democratically than the metropole did. It lasted two and a half years and ended in ashes.

statusPeriods.label: The Sierra Leone Company
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A London company of abolitionists and bankers appointed the governor, charged the settlers quit-rents on their own land, and ran courts they had no vote in — which is what the Nova Scotians rebelled against in 1800.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: The default 4 overstates it: the Company's writ ended at the edge of the peninsula, it was sacked by a French squadron in 1794, and it survived by treaty with Temne rulers and by the presence of the Royal Navy.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Freetown, under the Sierra Leone Company in London
statusPeriods.franchise: The settlers lost the vote they had held under Sharp's scheme. That loss, and the quit-rent, caused the 1800 rebellion.
statusPeriods.note: The Company's directors included Henry Thornton, William Wilberforce and Thomas Clarkson. An anti-slavery colony was run as a shareholders' venture and it went bankrupt.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony and anti-slavery base
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Crown took the bankrupt Company's colony and made Freetown the base of the Royal Navy squadron that stopped slave ships and of the courts that condemned them, landing the freed captives on the same peninsula.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Freetown, under the Colonial Office; also the seat of the Governor-in-Chief of the West African Settlements at various dates
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted for the Legislative Council until 1924, and then only in the Colony.
statusPeriods.note: Between 1808 and the 1860s something in the order of 90,000 to 100,000 people taken off captured slave ships were landed here. Their descendants, together with the Nova Scotians and Maroons, became the Krio.

statusPeriods.label: Colony and Protectorate
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: One governor ran two legal systems: a Crown colony of British subjects on the peninsula and a protectorate of British protected persons ruled through paramount chiefs and district commissioners inland.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Freetown, under the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.franchise: Three elected seats for the Colony from 1924. The 1951 constitution finally gave the Protectorate — 98 per cent of the population — a majority of seats, and power moved from the Krio to the interior in a single stroke.
statusPeriods.note: Fourah Bay College, founded in 1827 and affiliated to Durham University in 1876, made Freetown the place West Africans came to be educated. The Colony produced clerks, lawyers and bishops for the whole coast.

statusPeriods.label: Milton Margai's government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Milton Margai became Premier and Sierra Leonean ministers ran internal affairs while Britain kept defence and foreign policy until independence.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Freetown
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage in the Colony and a chiefdom-based indirect franchise in much of the Protectorate until 1957.
statusPeriods.note: The constitutional milestones here are less clean than Ghana's: the office of Premier dates from 1958 and full internal self-government is usually dated to the 1960 Lancaster House conference.

departures.how: After the Lancaster House conference of April-May 1960, Britain legislated Sierra Leone into independence and the flag changed in Freetown without a shot fired, though opposition leaders were detained for a general strike on the eve of it.

departures.borders: The borders were the ones France and Britain agreed in 1895 and Britain and Liberia in 1885: they cut Mende, Kissi and Kono communities into two and three countries, and independence did not move them.

acquisitions.how: English company agents built a fortified factory on an island in the estuary, well placed to buy captives brought down the Rokel and Port Loko rivers and to be defended from a single wall.

counterparties.name: The Temne and Bullom rulers of the estuary
counterparties.lost: They licensed the island and took rent and customs on its trade. What they lost was not land but control of who traded on their own river, once the fort had cannon on it.

people.name: Richard Oswald
people.role: Glasgow-born London merchant, principal owner of the island from 1748; negotiated the 1782 preliminary peace with Benjamin Franklin that recognised American independence

people.name: Henry Laurens
people.role: Charleston merchant and the island's American agent; sold its captives to South Carolina rice planters and later served as President of the Continental Congress

acquisitions.resistance: The island was attacked and burned repeatedly: by the French in 1704 and again in 1779, and by African rulers and traders when the agents cheated them or refused their customs.

contested.note: The founding date and the ownership history before 1748 are pieced together from fragmentary company records and are given differently in different accounts.

evidence.author: David Hancock
evidence.work: Citizens of the World: London Merchants and the Integration of the British Atlantic Community, 1735-1785
evidence.supports: Richard Oswald's syndicate, the running of Bunce Island and its Charleston connection.

from.note: The date the first English post on the island is usually given.

statusPeriods.label: A private British slave castle
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A handful of British agents held one walled island by paying rent to Temne and Bullom rulers, buying captives from African and Afro-European traders, and holding them in an open yard until a ship came.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: the owners' counting house in London
statusPeriods.note: Visitors described a golf course laid out for the agents on the island, with enslaved Africans carrying the clubs. The detail is often repeated and rests on eighteenth-century travellers' accounts.

statusPeriods.label: Abandoned, then a ruin in the Protectorate
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British abolition ended the island's business; a Freetown merchant ran a sawmill there into the 1830s and after that nobody governed it because nobody lived on it.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Freetown
statusPeriods.note: The buildings were left standing. That is why the slave yard, the fortified house and the graveyard survive to be walked through today.

departures.how: The island became Sierra Leonean at independence and was later declared a national monument; families in South Carolina and Georgia still trace ancestors through it.

led.name: Milton Margai
led.role: led Sierra Leone to independence

cost.note: Nobody died in 1961. The deaths that belong to this island were never recorded: captives who died in the yard were not entered in any ledger.

departures.borders: Nothing moved. The island is 30 kilometres from Freetown and has been in the same river for the whole story.

slavery.note: Bunce Island specialised: Carolina and Georgia planters paid extra for captives from the rice-growing Windward Coast, because they wanted people who already knew how to grow rice.

toll.note: No agreed total exists. Historians put the number shipped from the island over roughly 140 years in the tens of thousands; the company records that would settle it are incomplete.

populationTransfer.note: The people shipped from here went disproportionately to South Carolina and Georgia, and their descendants are the Gullah and Geechee communities of the American Sea Islands.

consequences.economicLegacy: The profits went to a London syndicate, and one of its partners used them to buy a Scottish estate and a seat at the table where American independence was negotiated.

evidence.author: David Hancock
evidence.work: Citizens of the World: London Merchants and the Integration of the British Atlantic Community, 1735-1785
evidence.supports: Oswald's syndicate, the island's business model and its Charleston market.

evidence.author: Christopher Fyfe
evidence.work: A History of Sierra Leone
evidence.supports: The island's place in the Sierra Leone estuary before and after 1808.

evidence.author: David Eltis and David Richardson
evidence.work: Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade
evidence.supports: Regional embarkation patterns for the Sierra Leone and Windward coasts.

contested.note: The island's early ownership and the total number of people shipped from it are both uncertain: the surviving records are partial and the estimates in circulation range widely.

pedagogy.hook: The man who owned this slave castle sat down in Paris in 1782 with Benjamin Franklin and negotiated American independence.

misconception.belief: The slave trade was carried on by a few disreputable men on the fringes of respectable British society.
misconception.correction: Richard Oswald owned Bunce Island, sat in London society, and was chosen by the British government to negotiate peace with the United States. His Charleston agent, Henry Laurens, became President of the Continental Congress. The trade ran through the centre of the Atlantic world's political class, not its margins.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Thirty kilometres separate Bunce Island from Freetown: a British slave castle and a British anti-slavery court, in the same estuary, in living memory of each other. Hold both facts at once and you understand the British record on slavery.

date.note: Fragmentary records; the founding year is approximate.

Richard Oswald's syndicate buys it and links it to Charleston
The Slave Trade Act ends the island's business
Becomes Sierra Leonean at independence

territories.name: Gold Coast
territories.formalName: The Gold Coast Colony, Ashanti and the Northern Territories
territories.subregion: Gulf of Guinea coast and the Volta basin

namesOverTime.name: Costa da Mina

to.note: The Portuguese name faded as Dutch and English traders took over; the date is a rough marker.

namesOverTime.note: 'The coast of the mine' — the gold came first, and gave the coast its European name.

namesOverTime.name: Ghana
namesOverTime.note: Chosen by Nkrumah after the medieval empire of Ghana, which lay some 1,500 km to the north-west in what is now Mali and Mauritania. The name was a claim about African history, not a description of the place.

modernSuccessors.name: Ghana
modernSuccessors.note: A republic since 1 July 1960. British Togoland joined it on the same day it became independent.

geoCoverage.label: Forts on a coast Britain did not govern
geoCoverage.change: A chain of stone forts, each renting its ground from the Fante, Fetu or Ga state around it. Britain owned buildings, not territory.

geoCoverage.label: The Gold Coast Colony
geoCoverage.change: Six months after burning Kumasi, Britain turned its 'protected territories' on the coast into a Crown colony without asking the states inside them.

geoCoverage.label: Colony, Ashanti and the Northern Territories
geoCoverage.change: Ashanti was annexed after the war of the Golden Stool and the north was declared a protectorate; the territory Britain claimed grew roughly fourfold in one Order in Council.

acquisitions.how: A London company holding a royal patent built a trading lodge at Kormantin on ground granted by the local ruler, to buy gold and, increasingly, people.

counterparties.name: The coastal Fante and Fetu states
counterparties.lost: Nothing at first: they granted the ground, took the rent and kept the sovereignty. What they gave up was exclusivity, and within a century their coast held some forty European forts within sight of one another.

people.name: Nicholas Crispe
people.role: London merchant whose 1631 patent began continuous English trade on the Gold Coast

contested.note: English ships had traded on this coast since the 1550s. 1631 is the conventional date for a permanent post, not for first contact.

evidence.author: William St Clair
evidence.work: The Grand Slave Emporium: Cape Coast Castle and the British Slave Trade
evidence.supports: The English arrival on the Gold Coast and the fort system.

acquisitions.how: Robert Holmes's squadron took the castle at Cape Coast from the Dutch, and the Treaty of Breda in 1667 confirmed it to England: it became the headquarters of English slave trading in Africa for 150 years.

counterparties.name: The Dutch West India Company
counterparties.lost: The Dutch lost their best harbour east of Elmina; their reprisals under De Ruyter took back most of the other English posts and helped start the Second Anglo-Dutch War.

counterparties.name: The state of Fetu
counterparties.lost: Fetu had licensed the ground to the Swedes, then the Danes, then the Dutch. Its ruler now dealt with a fourth set of tenants who paid rent and, in time, stopped paying.

instrument.name: Treaty of Breda
instrument.note: The same treaty in which the Dutch kept Suriname and the English kept New Amsterdam, which became New York.

people.name: Robert Holmes
people.role: naval captain who took Cape Coast Castle and several Dutch posts in 1664

acquisitions.how: Britain bought Denmark's five Gold Coast forts, including Christiansborg Castle at Accra, for £10,000 cash.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Denmark
counterparties.lost: Denmark, the first European state to outlaw its own slave trade in 1803, sold the forts it had no further use for and left Africa altogether.

counterparties.name: The Ga states of Accra and the Anlo of Keta
counterparties.lost: The people whose land the forts stood on were not parties to the sale and were not paid. Britain later taxed them under the poll tax of 1852 by right of a purchase from Denmark.

instrument.name: Anglo-Danish Convention for the cession of the Danish possessions on the coast of Guinea

acquisitions.how: The Netherlands handed Britain every Dutch fort on the coast, Elmina included, in exchange for a free hand against Aceh in Sumatra: two African towns and one Indonesian war changed hands in the same bargain.

counterparties.name: The Netherlands
counterparties.lost: The Dutch gave up 350 years on this coast, including São Jorge da Mina, the oldest European building in sub-Saharan Africa.

counterparties.name: The people of Elmina
counterparties.lost: Elmina's townspeople petitioned against being transferred and were ignored; in June 1873 British ships bombarded and burned much of their town.

counterparties.name: Asanteman (the Asante empire)
counterparties.lost: Asante had received an annual payment from the Dutch for Elmina and regarded the town as its outlet to the sea. Britain refused to pay it, and Asante invaded in 1873.

instrument.name: Anglo-Dutch Treaties of Sumatra
instrument.note: Signed in 1871, executed on the coast on 6 April 1872. The Dutch used their free hand to invade Aceh in 1873; Britain used its new possession to provoke a war with Asante in the same year.

acquisitions.how: Six months after Wolseley's column burned Kumasi, letters patent turned the coastal states Britain had called 'protected' since 1844 into a Crown colony with a governor over them.

counterparties.name: The Fante states and the Fante Confederation
counterparties.lost: The Fante had drafted their own constitution at Mankessim in 1871 for a self-governing confederation with schools, roads and taxes. Britain arrested its leaders for treason in December 1871 and annexed the coast three years later.

instrument.name: Letters patent constituting the Gold Coast Colony
instrument.note: Lagos was attached to the new colony until 1886.

people.name: Garnet Wolseley
people.role: commanded the 1873-74 expedition that burned Kumasi

people.name: John Mensah Sarbah
people.role: Fante barrister and historian whose Fanti Customary Laws (1897) argued in British courts that the land belonged to Africans

acquisitions.resistance: The Fante Confederation of 1868-73 was the resistance: an African-designed federal government on this coast, broken by British arrests before Britain declared its own.

acquisitions.how: After the siege of the Kumasi fort in 1900 was broken, Britain annexed Asante outright by Order in Council and ruled it from Kumasi as a separate territory under the same governor.

counterparties.name: Asanteman (the Asante empire)
counterparties.lost: Asante lost the independence it had held since about 1701, its Asantehene (already deported in 1896), and finally its status as a state; its Golden Stool was hidden and not surrendered.

instrument.name: Ashanti Order in Council 1901
instrument.note: Made on 26 September 1901 and brought into force on 1 January 1902.

acquisitions.resistance: Yaa Asantewaa, Queen Mother of Ejisu, led the 1900 rising that besieged the British fort at Kumasi for three months.

acquisitions.how: Britain declared a protectorate over the savannah north of Asante, on the strength of treaties its officers had raced French and German columns to sign in 1896-98, and governed it by a handful of commissioners.

counterparties.name: The Dagbon, Mamprugu, Gonja, Wa and Bulsa states and the stateless societies between them
counterparties.lost: Their rulers signed treaties they were told were friendship agreements and found they had signed away control of their own trade, courts and manpower.

instrument.name: Northern Territories Order in Council 1901
instrument.note: In force from 1 January 1902. The Anglo-French and Anglo-German boundary conventions of 1898-1899 had already drawn the lines.

acquisitions.resistance: Samori Ture's forces and the Zabarima raiders were fighting through this country in the 1890s; British columns spent years burning compounds in the north-east before administration settled.

statusPeriods.label: Forts of the slave-trading companies
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Royal African Company and its successors held about ten stone forts, paid ground rent to the states around them, and had no jurisdiction over anyone who was not inside their walls.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Cape Coast Castle, under the company's court of assistants in London
statusPeriods.note: The Royal African Company held the monopoly from 1672 to 1698 and the forts until 1752; the African Company of Merchants ran them on a parliamentary grant until 1821.

statusPeriods.label: Crown forts attached to Sierra Leone
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Parliament abolished the African Company and vested the forts in the Crown under the governor at Freetown; within three years the governor had been killed fighting Asante and London wanted out.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Freetown
statusPeriods.note: Sir Charles MacCarthy was killed at Nsamankow in January 1824 and his skull was kept as an Asante trophy. Britain lost the first Anglo-Asante war.

statusPeriods.label: Handed back to a merchants' committee
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain gave up: the forts went to a London committee of merchants on a £4,000 annual grant, and their president at Cape Coast, George Maclean, built an informal jurisdiction over the Fante states by arbitrating their disputes.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Cape Coast Castle, under a committee of merchants in London
statusPeriods.note: Maclean's peace with Asante in 1831 held for thirty years. A British official with no legal authority and no army governed more effectively than the Crown had, which is why Parliament took the forts back.

statusPeriods.label: Crown forts and the Bond of 1844
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Crown resumed the forts and, in the Bond of 1844, got eight Fante chiefs to sign an acknowledgement of British jurisdiction over serious crimes — the whole legal basis for what came next.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Cape Coast Castle, under the Colonial Office or Freetown at different dates
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. A poll tax imposed in 1852 by an assembly of chiefs collapsed in resistance within a few years.
statusPeriods.note: In 1865 a parliamentary select committee formally recommended withdrawal from all West African settlements except Sierra Leone. Nine years later Britain annexed the Gold Coast instead.

statusPeriods.label: Crown colony, then colony plus Ashanti and the north
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor at Accra ruled through district commissioners and, after 1925, through chiefs given statutory 'native authority' powers; an African-majority Legislative Council existed from 1946 but the governor held the veto.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Cape Coast until 1877, then Accra
statusPeriods.franchise: Three elected municipal seats from 1925, on a property franchise in Accra, Cape Coast and Sekondi. The Burns constitution of 1946 gave Africans an elected majority for the first time in any British African colony; the 1951 election was the first mass vote.
statusPeriods.note: In 1948 the Gold Coast was, on paper, Britain's model African colony: cocoa-rich, peaceful, with the best schools in West Africa. On 28 February 1948 police shot ex-servicemen marching to Christiansborg and the model fell apart in three days of riots.

statusPeriods.label: Nkrumah's government under a British governor
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Nkrumah won the 1951 election from a prison cell, was released to lead the government, and by 1954 ran an all-African cabinet while the governor kept defence, foreign affairs and police.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Accra
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage for the elected seats from 1951 — the first mass electorate in colonial Africa.
statusPeriods.note: The three elections of 1951, 1954 and 1956 were all won by the Convention People's Party. Britain demanded the third one before conceding independence, to test whether the CPP still had a mandate.

departures.how: After three elections, a general strike, a prison term and eight years of organised mass politics, the Gold Coast became Ghana at midnight on 6 March 1957: the first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to take its independence from a European power.

led.name: Kwame Nkrumah
led.role: founded the Convention People's Party in 1949, called Positive Action in 1950, won the 1951 election from James Fort prison, and became Prime Minister and then President

led.name: J.B. Danquah
led.role: lawyer and scholar who founded the United Gold Coast Convention in 1947, invited Nkrumah home to organise it, then opposed him; died in detention under Nkrumah in 1965

led.name: Kobina Sekyi
led.role: Cape Coast lawyer and Aborigines' Rights Protection Society leader whose generation fought colonial land law for decades before mass politics arrived

led.name: Charles Arden-Clarke
led.role: last British governor; released Nkrumah from prison in 1951 and worked with him for six years

departures.movement: Convention People's Party, out of the United Gold Coast Convention

cost.note: The Accra riots of 28 February to 3 March 1948, which began the mass movement, left 29 people dead and over 200 injured according to the Watson Commission of inquiry. No one was killed at independence itself.

warrant.author: Aiken Watson and the Commission of Enquiry into Disturbances in the Gold Coast
warrant.work: Report of the Commission of Enquiry into Disturbances in the Gold Coast, 1948 (Colonial No. 231)
warrant.supports: 29 people killed and more than 200 injured in the Accra riots of 28 February to 3 March 1948.

departures.borders: Ghana inherited three separate British territories plus a UN trust territory, welded into one state on the day. The northern boundary with Upper Volta and the eastern one with Togo were drawn by Anglo-French conventions in 1898 and 1919 and cut Dagomba, Ewe and Konkomba country in two.

instrument.name: Ghana Independence Act 1957
instrument.note: Royal assent 7 February 1957; independence took effect on 6 March 1957, the 113th anniversary of the Bond of 1844.

evidence.author: Dennis Austin
evidence.work: Politics in Ghana, 1946-1960
evidence.supports: The rise of the CPP, the three elections and the transfer of power.

slavery.note: Roughly 1.2 million people were shipped into the Atlantic trade from this coast, a large share of them through British forts, and the Asante and coastal states that sold them grew rich on it.

emancipationDate.note: Ordinances of 1874 abolished slave-dealing and emancipated people held in slavery inside the new colony. Enforcement was slow and pawning persisted for decades.

toll.note: The Gold Coast regional embarkation total comes from the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database and is an estimate reconstructed from surviving voyage records; it is a floor, not a ceiling.

violence.note: Britain and Asante fought five wars between 1823 and 1900; British columns burned Kumasi twice, in 1874 and 1896, and deported the Asantehene.

commonwealth.note: A republic from 1 July 1960 and still a Commonwealth member. Ghana's decision, like India's, showed a republic could stay in.

consequences.economicLegacy: Cocoa made the colony rich and it was grown entirely by African smallholders who bought their own seedlings; by 1911 the Gold Coast was the world's largest producer, and the money paid for the schools that produced the men who ended British rule.
consequences.borderLegacy: Ghana's borders come from Anglo-French and Anglo-German conventions of 1898-1919 and split Ewe, Dagomba and Konkomba communities across three countries.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English law sits beside Akan, Ga, Ewe and Dagbani customary law, and the chieftaincy Britain reorganised in 1925 and 1935 is written into Ghana's constitution.

peak.populationNote: 1948 census of the Gold Coast. With British Togoland, independent Ghana covered 238,533 km² and counted 6,726,815 people in the 1960 census.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Gold Coast’s largest recorded population: 4,118,450 people, counted in 1948.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Dennis Austin
evidence.work: Politics in Ghana, 1946-1960
evidence.supports: The politics of decolonisation and the CPP's three election victories.

evidence.author: David Kimble
evidence.work: A Political History of Ghana: The Rise of Gold Coast Nationalism, 1850-1928
evidence.supports: The Fante Confederation, the Aborigines' Rights Protection Society and early nationalism.

evidence.author: William St Clair
evidence.work: The Grand Slave Emporium: Cape Coast Castle and the British Slave Trade
evidence.supports: The forts, the Royal African Company and the working of the trade.

contested.note: Historians argue about why Britain conceded so fast here: whether Nkrumah's mass movement forced the pace, whether the Colonial Office had already decided the Gold Coast was the safest place to try self-government, or whether cocoa revenue made a cooperative Ghana more useful than a resentful colony.

pedagogy.hook: Ghana chose 6 March for its independence day because that was the date, 113 years earlier, on which Fante chiefs had signed away their jurisdiction to Britain.

misconception.belief: Europeans developed colonial economies; Africans provided the labour.
misconception.correction: Nobody in London planned Gold Coast cocoa. African farmers bought the seedlings, cleared their own forest and financed their own transport, and by 1911 the colony was the largest producer on earth. There were no European cocoa plantations. The colonial state taxed the crop, and its marketing board later kept the gap between the world price and what it paid farmers.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: This is where the empire in Africa ended first. Everything that happened between 1948 and 1957 — the riots, the party, the prison sentence, the elections — became the template that Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Kenya and Tanganyika followed, and it made Nkrumah the most listened-to African of his generation.

territories.name: Cape Coast Castle
territories.formalName: Cape Coast Castle, headquarters of the British forts on the Gold Coast

namesOverTime.name: Carolusborg
namesOverTime.note: Built by the Swedish Africa Company and named after Charles X; it changed hands five times in eleven years.

namesOverTime.name: Cape Coast Castle
namesOverTime.note: From the Portuguese Cabo Corso, 'short cape', which the English heard as Cape Coast.

namesOverTime.name: Oguaa

from.note: A rough marker for the pre-contact period, not an event.

namesOverTime.note: The Fante name of the town, still in daily use.

modernSuccessors.name: Ghana
modernSuccessors.note: A UNESCO World Heritage Site. Barack and Michelle Obama walked through the dungeons in July 2009.

geoCoverage.label: One castle and its parade ground
geoCoverage.change: No geo unit exists at this scale; the map hatches the Gold Coast littoral and marks the castle with a point.

acquisitions.how: Robert Holmes stormed the castle the Swedes had built and the Dutch had taken, and England kept it: from 1672 it was the head office of the Royal African Company and the largest slave-holding fort on the coast.

counterparties.name: The Dutch West India Company
counterparties.lost: The Dutch lost the castle they had held for less than a year and struck back so hard across the coast that the Second Anglo-Dutch War followed.

counterparties.name: The state of Fetu
counterparties.lost: Fetu's ruler had granted the ground and taken rent from Swedes, Danes and Dutch in turn. The English tenancy became permanent and eventually stopped being a tenancy at all.

people.name: Robert Holmes
people.role: took the castle for the Company of Royal Adventurers in 1664

evidence.author: William St Clair
evidence.work: The Grand Slave Emporium: Cape Coast Castle and the British Slave Trade
evidence.supports: The castle's capture, its rebuilding and its operation as the company headquarters.

statusPeriods.label: Headquarters of the Royal African Company
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor-in-chief and a council of company servants ran the castle, bought captives from Fante and Asante traders, and held them in vaulted dungeons cut into the rock until a ship anchored in the roads.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: the Royal African Company, then the African Company of Merchants, in London
statusPeriods.note: The Anglican chapel was built directly above the male dungeon. Philip Quaque, a Fante boy educated in England and ordained in 1765 as the first African priest of the Church of England, preached in it and ran a school in the castle for fifty years.

statusPeriods.label: Vested in the Crown
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Parliament abolished the African Company and the castle became government property under the governor at Freetown.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Freetown

statusPeriods.label: George Maclean's court
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A merchants' committee held the castle on a government grant, and its president George Maclean judged Fante disputes brought to him voluntarily, building a jurisdiction he had no legal right to exercise.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Cape Coast Castle, under a merchants' committee in London
statusPeriods.note: Maclean's wife was the poet Letitia Elizabeth Landon, who died of prussic acid in the castle in October 1838, two months after arriving. Nobody has ever settled whether it was suicide, accident or murder.

statusPeriods.label: Seat of government, then a monument
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The castle was the seat of British government on the Gold Coast until the capital moved to Accra in 1877, and after that a prison, offices, a school and finally a museum.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Cape Coast, then Accra

departures.how: The castle passed to Ghana at independence and became a museum of the trade that built it, run by the descendants of the people who were sold from it and of those who sold them.

led.name: Kwame Nkrumah
led.role: led the Gold Coast to independence

cost.note: Nobody died in 1957. Between 1664 and 1807 an unknown number of people died inside these walls before ever boarding a ship, and no register of them was kept.

departures.borders: Nothing moved. The castle's walls are where they were in 1664 and the sea is taking them slowly.

slavery.note: The dungeons held several hundred people at a time in the dark, for weeks, until a ship came; the governor's rooms were directly above them and the chapel above that.

toll.note: No total exists for the castle alone. Around 1.2 million people were shipped from the Gold Coast as a whole, and Cape Coast was the largest British holding point on it for over a century.

consequences.economicLegacy: The castle is now one of the most visited sites in West Africa, and Ghana's 'Year of Return' in 2019 built a tourism policy around African-American and Caribbean people coming to walk through it.

evidence.author: William St Clair
evidence.work: The Grand Slave Emporium: Cape Coast Castle and the British Slave Trade
evidence.supports: The castle's construction, garrison, dungeons and business, from the company's own records.

evidence.author: William A. Pettigrew
evidence.work: Freedom's Debt: The Royal African Company and the Politics of the Atlantic Slave Trade, 1672-1752
evidence.supports: The Royal African Company's monopoly, its politics and its scale.

pedagogy.hook: The Anglican chapel at Cape Coast Castle was built directly on top of the dungeon where hundreds of people were held in the dark waiting for a ship.

misconception.belief: The slave castles were where Europeans imprisoned people they had captured in raids.
misconception.correction: Almost nobody in these dungeons was captured by a European. They were bought: taken in wars and raids by African states — Asante, Denkyira, Akwamu, Fante — and marched to the coast by African traders who sold them for guns, cloth, iron and cowries. That does not reduce British responsibility; it explains why the trade could reach the scale it did.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Cape Coast Castle is the physical machine of the British slave trade: purchasing hall, holding cells, chapel, cannon and counting house in one building. Standing in it makes the abstraction of 'the triangular trade' concrete in a way no diagram does.
