Robert Holmes takes it for England
It becomes headquarters of the Royal African Company
The capital moves to Accra; the castle becomes a prison
Passes to independent Ghana

territories.name: Elmina
territories.formalName: St George's Castle, Elmina

namesOverTime.name: São Jorge da Mina
namesOverTime.note: Begun in January 1482 with stone shipped from Portugal: the oldest European building still standing south of the Sahara.

namesOverTime.name: Elmina
namesOverTime.note: The Dutch contraction of da Mina, 'the mine'.

from.note: A rough marker for when the Fante name is first recorded, not an event.

modernSuccessors.name: Ghana
modernSuccessors.note: A UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979, together with Cape Coast Castle and the other Gold Coast forts.

geoCoverage.label: A castle and the town beneath it
geoCoverage.change: No geo unit exists at this scale; the map hatches the Gold Coast littoral and marks Elmina with a point.

acquisitions.how: The Dutch flag came down at Elmina and the British went up, under a treaty in which Britain traded away its claims in Sumatra so the Netherlands could make war on Aceh.

counterparties.name: The Netherlands
counterparties.lost: The Dutch gave up the castle they had taken from Portugal in 1637 and every other post on the coast, ending 235 years there.

counterparties.name: The people of Elmina
counterparties.lost: Elmina's townspeople, long allied to the Dutch and to Asante, petitioned against the transfer, refused British authority, and had their town shelled and burned by British forces in June 1873.

counterparties.name: Asanteman (the Asante empire)
counterparties.lost: Asante lost the annual payment the Dutch had made for Elmina and its recognised outlet to the sea. Britain called the payment rent for a Dutch tenancy; Asante called it tribute for Asante land. The war of 1873-74 followed.

instrument.name: Anglo-Dutch Treaties of Sumatra
instrument.note: One treaty caused two wars on opposite sides of the world: the Dutch invaded Aceh in 1873 and the British invaded Asante in the same year.

acquisitions.resistance: The Elminas fought the British landing party in 1873 and their town was destroyed by naval bombardment and demolition.

evidence.author: Ivor Wilks
evidence.work: Asante in the Nineteenth Century: The Structure and Evolution of a Political Order
evidence.supports: The Elmina note, Asante's claim to the town, and the origins of the 1873 war.

statusPeriods.label: British castle and district headquarters
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The castle became a British district headquarters, prison and, later, a police training school; the town was rebuilt under British authority after 1873 with its Asante-allied leadership removed.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Cape Coast, then Accra
statusPeriods.note: In 1873 the British deported the Elmina leaders they thought pro-Asante and destroyed the town; the community has never fully recovered its former position on the coast.

departures.how: Elmina became part of independent Ghana, and the castle Portugal built in 1482 passed to an African government for the first time in 475 years.

led.name: Kwame Nkrumah
led.role: led the Gold Coast to independence

cost.note: Nobody died in 1957. Elmina's dead belong to 1873, when the town was shelled and burned, and to the four centuries of the trade before that.

departures.borders: Nothing moved on the ground.

slavery.note: Elmina was the first and the longest-running European slave-trading castle in Africa: Portuguese, then Dutch, and by the time the British got it in 1872 the Atlantic trade was over.

abolitionDate.note: Britain's abolition. The Netherlands abolished its slave trade in 1814 and slavery in its colonies only in 1863.

violence.note: The British burned Elmina town in June 1873 after its people refused to accept the transfer and were suspected of supporting Asante.

consequences.economicLegacy: The castle is a World Heritage Site and one of Ghana's most visited buildings.

evidence.author: Ivor Wilks
evidence.work: Asante in the Nineteenth Century: The Structure and Evolution of a Political Order
evidence.supports: Elmina's relationship with Asante and the causes of the 1873 war.

evidence.author: William St Clair
evidence.work: The Grand Slave Emporium: Cape Coast Castle and the British Slave Trade
evidence.supports: The rivalry of the Gold Coast forts and the trade they ran.

pedagogy.hook: Britain got Elmina by giving the Dutch a free hand to invade Aceh in Sumatra — one treaty, two wars, opposite sides of the world.

misconception.belief: European powers grabbed African territory directly from Africans during the Scramble.
misconception.correction: A great deal of it was traded between Europeans, sometimes for something on another continent entirely. Britain swapped its Sumatran claims for the Dutch Gold Coast in 1871, bought Denmark's forts in 1850 for £10,000, and gave Heligoland to Germany in 1890 for Zanzibar. Africans were the subject of these deals and never a party to them.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Elmina links the empire's continents: the same document that put a British flag on this castle sent Dutch troops into Aceh, and the Asante war that followed shaped Ghana's borders. Imperial decisions were traded, not made in isolation.

keyDates.what: Portugal builds São Jorge da Mina, the oldest European building in tropical Africa
The Dutch take it
Handed to Britain under the Anglo-Dutch Treaties of Sumatra
British forces shell and burn Elmina town
Passes to independent Ghana

territories.name: The Danish Gold Coast forts
territories.formalName: Christiansborg and the former Danish possessions on the Gold Coast
territories.subregion: Accra plains and the lower Volta

namesOverTime.name: Christiansborg
namesOverTime.note: Built by Denmark at Osu in 1661 on ground bought from the Ga; the name stuck through British rule and Ghanaian independence.

namesOverTime.name: Osu Castle
namesOverTime.note: The seat of Ghana's government until 2013.

geoCoverage.label: Five forts from Accra to Keta
geoCoverage.change: No geo unit exists at this scale; the map hatches the Gold Coast littoral and marks the forts with points.

acquisitions.how: Britain paid Denmark £10,000 for Christiansborg Castle at Accra and four smaller forts along the coast to Keta, and Denmark left Africa for good.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Denmark
counterparties.lost: Denmark sold nearly two centuries of Gold Coast presence for a sum that would have bought a large London house, because its forts had no purpose after it abolished its own slave trade in 1803.

counterparties.name: The Ga states of Osu and Accra and the Anlo Ewe of Keta
counterparties.lost: They had leased the ground to Denmark and were neither consulted nor paid when the leases were sold. Britain then taxed them under the 1852 poll tax as if the purchase had bought their allegiance too.

instrument.name: Anglo-Danish Convention for the cession of the Danish possessions on the coast of Guinea
instrument.note: £10,000 was paid for the forts and the buildings, not for sovereignty over the people around them — a distinction Britain then ignored.

acquisitions.resistance: The poll tax of 1852, levied on the strength of the purchase, was resisted from the start and had collapsed by 1861; Britain shelled Anlo towns near Keta in the 1860s and 1870s.

statusPeriods.label: British forts, then the seat of government
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Christiansborg became a British fort, then in 1877 the governor's residence and the seat of the Gold Coast government, which it stayed until independence and beyond.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Christiansborg Castle, Accra
statusPeriods.note: On 28 February 1948 police fired on ex-servicemen marching to the castle to present a petition, killing three of them. The Accra riots that followed began the movement that ended British rule.

departures.how: Christiansborg passed to Ghana at independence and Nkrumah governed from the same rooms the British governor had used, on ground the Ga had leased to Denmark in 1661.

led.name: Kwame Nkrumah
led.role: led the Gold Coast to independence and made Christiansborg his seat of government

led.name: Cornelius Adjetey
led.role: ex-serviceman shot dead by police outside the castle on 28 February 1948; a monument to him stands at the spot

cost.note: Nobody died in 1957. Three ex-servicemen were killed outside this castle on 28 February 1948, and 29 people died in the riots that followed, according to the Watson Commission.

departures.borders: Nothing moved.

slavery.note: Denmark shipped roughly 100,000 people from these forts before it became, in 1803, the first European state to abolish its own Atlantic slave trade.

abolitionDate.note: The Danish decree of 1792 took effect in 1803, four years before the British Act.

toll.note: Danish embarkation estimates come from the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database and are reconstructions from surviving voyage records.

consequences.economicLegacy: Osu Castle housed Ghana's head of state until 2013 and is now a museum: the building the empire governed from became the building independence governed from.

evidence.author: David Kimble
evidence.work: A Political History of Ghana: The Rise of Gold Coast Nationalism, 1850-1928
evidence.supports: The 1850 purchase, the poll tax and the extension of British authority east of Accra.

evidence.author: Roger S. Gocking
evidence.work: The History of Ghana
evidence.supports: Christiansborg's later role and the 1948 shootings.

pedagogy.hook: Britain bought a fifth of the Gold Coast's forts from Denmark for £10,000, then taxed the people living around them on the grounds that it had bought them too.

misconception.belief: Britain was the first country to abolish the slave trade.
misconception.correction: Denmark was. Its 1792 decree took effect in 1803, four years before the British Act of 1807. Denmark's trade was much smaller, which is part of why abolishing it was easier — but 'first' is a claim that can be checked, and it is not Britain's.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The castle in this record is where the empire ended and Ghana began, in the same building: the governor's residence became the President's, and the men shot outside its gates in 1948 are why.

keyDates.what: Denmark builds Christiansborg at Osu
Denmark's abolition of its slave trade takes effect
Britain buys the Danish forts for £10,000
Police shoot marching ex-servicemen at the castle crossroads
Nkrumah takes office in the governor's castle

territories.name: Ashanti
territories.formalName: The Colony of Ashanti

namesOverTime.name: Asanteman

from.note: The date usually given for the union of the Akan states under Osei Tutu; the founding was a process, not a day.

namesOverTime.note: 'The Asante nation'. Its people are Asante; 'Ashanti' is the British spelling and survives as the name of a Ghanaian region.

modernSuccessors.name: Ghana
modernSuccessors.note: The Asantehene is still enthroned at Manhyia in Kumasi and the Golden Stool has never been surrendered.

geoCoverage.label: Occupied, with the Asantehene deported
geoCoverage.change: A British column occupied Kumasi and deported the Asantehene, but Asante was not annexed and much of it was not administered at all.

geoCoverage.label: Annexed British territory
geoCoverage.change: After the 1900 rising was crushed, an Order in Council annexed Asante outright and put a Chief Commissioner in Kumasi.

acquisitions.how: A British expedition marched on Kumasi and the Asantehene Agyeman Prempeh I submitted without fighting to save the city; he was arrested anyway, with his mother and his chiefs, and deported.

counterparties.name: Asanteman (the Asante empire)
counterparties.lost: Asante lost its king, its treasury and its independence in a single afternoon without a battle. Prempeh I spent 28 years in exile — at Elmina, in Sierra Leone, then in the Seychelles from 1900.

people.name: Agyeman Prempeh I
people.role: Asantehene; submitted in 1896 to spare Kumasi, was deported for 28 years, and returned in 1924 as a private citizen

people.name: Francis Scott
people.role: commanded the 1895-96 expedition to Kumasi

people.name: Yaa Kyaa
people.role: Asantehemaa and Prempeh's mother; deported with him

acquisitions.resistance: Asante had already fought Britain in 1823-31, 1863-64 and 1873-74. In 1896 the Asantehene calculated that submission would preserve Kumasi, and Britain deported him regardless.

evidence.author: Ivor Wilks
evidence.work: Asante in the Nineteenth Century: The Structure and Evolution of a Political Order
evidence.supports: Asante statecraft, its wars with Britain and the 1896 submission.

acquisitions.how: After the rising of 1900 was broken, Britain annexed Asante by Order in Council and governed it from Kumasi as conquered territory under a Chief Commissioner.

counterparties.name: Asanteman (the Asante empire)
counterparties.lost: A state two centuries old, with a standing army, a civil service, a road network and tributaries from the coast to the Volta, ceased to exist in law.

instrument.name: Ashanti Order in Council 1901
instrument.note: In force from 1 January 1902.

acquisitions.resistance: The war of the Golden Stool: Yaa Asantewaa, Queen Mother of Ejisu, led the chiefs who besieged the British fort at Kumasi from April to July 1900.

cost.note: Roughly 1,000 dead on the British side, most of them African soldiers and carriers and many of them from disease, and around 2,000 Asante. The figures come from British military reports; no Asante count was taken and the totals are estimates.

warrant.author: The British columns, in their own military reports
warrant.work: British military reports of the Asante campaign of 1900
warrant.supports: Roughly 1,000 dead on the British side, most of them African soldiers and carriers and many of them from disease, and around 2,000 Asante. The figures come from British military reports; no Asante count was taken and the totals are estimates.
warrant.check: Campaign returns, casualty states and despatches are in the WO, ADM and CO series at The National Archives, Kew; the despatches were printed in the London Gazette and the totals in British Parliamentary Papers.
warrant.note: The side doing the killing counted its own dead precisely and the other side’s by estimate. That asymmetry is in the figure, not just in the footnote.

evidence.author: A. Adu Boahen
evidence.work: Yaa Asantewaa and the Asante-British War of 1900-1
evidence.supports: The 1900 rising, its leadership and its suppression.

statusPeriods.label: Kumasi under a British Resident
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British Resident sat in a fort in Kumasi with no king to work through and no clear legal authority; the chiefs were left in place and told what to do, and in 1900 they stopped listening.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: the fort at Kumasi, under the governor at Accra
statusPeriods.note: In March 1900 Governor Frederick Hodgson came to Kumasi, demanded the Golden Stool and asked why it had not been produced for him to sit on. It was the single most efficient recruiting speech in the history of Asante resistance.

statusPeriods.label: Conquered territory under a Chief Commissioner
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Chief Commissioner at Kumasi ruled through individual chiefs deliberately kept separate, so that no Asante authority above the level of a single town could re-form.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kumasi, under the governor at Accra
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. Asante had no representation in the Gold Coast Legislative Council until 1946.
statusPeriods.note: The Golden Stool was never handed over. In 1920 railway workers found its hiding place and stripped its gold; the men responsible were tried by Asante courts and Britain, alarmed, agreed the stool was sacred and let the case proceed.

statusPeriods.label: The Asante Confederacy restored
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain restored the Asante Confederacy and the office of Asantehene as a native authority under indirect rule, thirty-three years after abolishing them and after concluding that ruling without them cost more than it saved.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kumasi, under the governor at Accra
statusPeriods.franchise: Asante got seats in the Gold Coast Legislative Council under the 1946 Burns constitution and voted in the mass elections of 1951, 1954 and 1956.
statusPeriods.note: Prempeh I had already been allowed home in 1924 and made Kumasihene in 1926. His successor Prempeh II became Asantehene of a restored confederacy in 1935 — a British invention of an African tradition that the Asante had never stopped believing in.

departures.how: Asante left British rule inside Ghana, having spent the previous three years campaigning for a federal constitution that would have kept Kumasi's cocoa money in Kumasi, and having lost that argument.

led.name: Baffuor Osei Akoto
led.role: linguist to the Asantehene and founder of the National Liberation Movement in 1954, which demanded federalism for Asante

led.name: Kwame Nkrumah
led.role: insisted on a unitary Ghana and won the 1956 election that decided it

led.name: Otumfuo Osei Agyeman Prempeh II
led.role: Asantehene from 1931; supported the federalist case without leading it

departures.movement: National Liberation Movement (for federalism); Convention People's Party (for a unitary state)

cost.note: Political violence between NLM and CPP supporters in Ashanti between 1954 and 1956 killed a small number of people; no reliable total was compiled. Nobody died at independence itself.

departures.borders: Asante's borders as drawn by Britain in 1902 became internal Ghanaian boundaries. Britain refused the NLM's demand for a federal constitution and required a third election in 1956 before conceding independence, which the CPP won.

contested.note: Historians disagree about the National Liberation Movement: whether it was a cocoa-price revolt, an Asante nationalist movement, or a chieftaincy defending its position against a modernising party. All three readings have evidence behind them.

violence.note: Britain and Asante fought five wars in 77 years; the British burned Kumasi in 1874 and occupied it in 1896, deported its king for 28 years, and crushed the 1900 rising.

toll.note: For the 1900 war only, and an estimate: British military returns counted their own dead, mostly African soldiers and carriers, and nobody counted Asante dead.

slavery.note: Asante was a major supplier to the Atlantic trade and used enslaved labour at home; British abolition cut its export market and pushed it towards gold and kola.

emancipationDate.note: Slavery in Asante was formally abolished under British rule in stages; pawning and servile labour persisted well into the twentieth century.

consequences.economicLegacy: Asante gold went from an African state monopoly to a British concession company: Ashanti Goldfields was founded in 1897 on a grant from the chief of Adansi and became one of the richest mines in the empire.
consequences.languageAndLaw: The Asantehene, the Golden Stool and the Asanteman Council survive as a constitutionally recognised institution in Ghana — a state Britain abolished in 1902 and restored in 1935.

peak.populationNote: Colonial Ashanti covered more than the modern Ashanti Region and its population is not cleanly separable from Gold Coast census totals; the 1948 count for Ashanti is usually given as something under a million.

evidence.author: Ivor Wilks
evidence.work: Asante in the Nineteenth Century: The Structure and Evolution of a Political Order
evidence.supports: The structure of the Asante state and its dealings with Britain.

evidence.author: A. Adu Boahen
evidence.work: Yaa Asantewaa and the Asante-British War of 1900-1
evidence.supports: The 1900 rising and Yaa Asantewaa's leadership.

evidence.author: T.C. McCaskie
evidence.work: State and Society in Pre-colonial Asante
evidence.supports: Asante society, the Golden Stool and the meaning of the 1900 demand.

pedagogy.hook: In 1900 a British governor sat down in Kumasi and demanded the Golden Stool to sit on. A sixty-year-old woman raised an army over it.

misconception.belief: African states fell quickly to European armies because of the machine gun.
misconception.correction: Asante fought Britain in 1823, 1863, 1873, 1896 and 1900. It won the first war outright — a British governor was killed and his skull kept as a trophy in 1824 — and it was still capable of besieging a British garrison for three months in 1900, seventy-seven years after the fighting began. Conquest here took most of a century.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Asante shows what a West African state was: a written civil service, a road system, a treasury, an army and a two-hundred-year history. Colonial conquest was not the arrival of government in a place without one.

date.note: The union of the Akan states was a process; the date is conventional.

keyDates.what: Osei Tutu unites the Akan states; the Golden Stool
Asante destroys a British force at Nsamankow and kills Governor MacCarthy
Wolseley's column burns Kumasi
Prempeh I submits and is deported for 28 years
Hodgson demands the Golden Stool; Yaa Asantewaa's war begins
Britain restores the Asante Confederacy it abolished in 1902

territories.name: Northern Territories of the Gold Coast
territories.formalName: The Northern Territories of the Gold Coast Protectorate

namesOverTime.name: The Northern Territories
namesOverTime.note: A name that describes where it is from Accra, and says nothing about the Dagbon, Mamprugu, Gonja, Wa and Bulsa states inside it.

namesOverTime.name: The northern regions of Ghana
namesOverTime.note: Now the Northern, North East, Savannah, Upper East and Upper West regions of Ghana.

modernSuccessors.name: Ghana
modernSuccessors.note: Now Ghana's Northern, Savannah, North East, Upper East and Upper West regions — still the poorest part of the country.

geoCoverage.label: A protectorate administered by a handful of officers
geoCoverage.change: About 70,000 square kilometres claimed on the strength of treaties signed in a race against French and German columns in 1896-98, and administered thinly for the next 55 years.

acquisitions.how: Britain declared a protectorate over the savannah north of Asante, on the strength of treaties its officers had raced French and German expeditions to sign with rulers who were told they were agreements of friendship.

counterparties.name: Dagbon, Mamprugu, Gonja, Wa and the stateless societies of the north-east
counterparties.lost: The Ya-Na of Dagbon and the other rulers lost control of their trade routes, their courts' jurisdiction over serious crime and their independence; the Talensi, Kusasi, Frafra and other societies without kings had chiefs invented for them by British officers to have someone to give orders to.

counterparties.name: France and Germany
counterparties.lost: Both had columns in the field claiming the same country. The boundaries agreed in 1898 and 1899 cut Dagomba, Mamprusi and Konkomba country between three empires.

instrument.name: Northern Territories Order in Council 1901
instrument.note: In force from 1 January 1902; the boundaries had been settled by Anglo-French and Anglo-German conventions in 1898 and 1899.

people.name: George Ekem Ferguson
people.role: Fante surveyor in British service who signed most of the northern treaties for Britain and was killed at Wa in 1897

people.name: Babatu
people.role: Zabarima slave-raiding commander whose forces were fighting across the north-east when the British arrived

acquisitions.resistance: British columns spent a decade burning compounds in the north-east; the Talensi resisted from the Tongo hills until 1911, and forced labour on roads provoked repeated flight across the French border.

evidence.author: Roger S. Gocking
evidence.work: The History of Ghana
evidence.supports: The occupation of the north and its administration as a labour reserve.

statusPeriods.label: A labour reserve under a Chief Commissioner
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A Chief Commissioner at Tamale governed through chiefs, some of them ancient and some invented for the purpose, and the territory's declared purpose in official policy was to supply men to the mines and cocoa farms of the south.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Gambaga, then Tamale from 1907, under the governor at Accra
statusPeriods.franchise: The Northern Territories had no elected representation of any kind until 1951, and no seats in the Gold Coast Legislative Council before 1946.
statusPeriods.note: Britain deliberately spent almost nothing here. The first secondary school in the Northern Territories opened in 1951, 49 years after the protectorate was declared and 76 years after the first one on the coast.

departures.how: The Northern Territories became part of Ghana at independence, joined to a south whose schools, roads, railways and cocoa money they had been kept out of for two generations.

led.name: Simon Diedong Dombo
led.role: founder of the Northern People's Party in 1954, which demanded protection for northern interests in an independent Ghana

led.name: Kwame Nkrumah
led.role: led the Gold Coast to independence on a unitary constitution

departures.movement: Northern People's Party, then absorbed into the United Party

cost.note: Nobody died at independence. The cost of this territory was paid over 55 years in schools not built and men sent south to work.

departures.borders: The 1898 Anglo-French and 1899 Anglo-German lines became Ghana's northern and eastern borders, splitting Dagomba, Mamprusi, Bissa and Konkomba country between Ghana, Burkina Faso and Togo.

populationTransfer.note: Colonial policy made the north a labour reserve: tens of thousands of men walked south each year to the mines and cocoa farms, a migration pattern that still shapes Ghana.

violence.note: The occupation of the north-east was carried out by burning compounds and seizing livestock; the Talensi held out in the Tongo hills until 1911.

consequences.borderLegacy: Ghana's northern border with Burkina Faso and its eastern border with Togo were drawn in Paris, London and Berlin in 1898-99 and cut through Dagomba, Mamprusi and Konkomba country.
consequences.economicLegacy: The north-south development gap in Ghana is not an accident of geography. It was policy: revenue was raised in the north and spent in the south, and the north's export was men.

peak.populationNote: The Northern Territories held roughly a fifth of the Gold Coast's people. Ghana's 1960 census counted about 1.29 million in the successor Northern and Upper regions.

evidence.author: Roger S. Gocking
evidence.work: The History of Ghana
evidence.supports: The administration of the Northern Territories and the origins of Ghana's regional inequality.

evidence.author: Michael Crowder
evidence.work: West Africa under Colonial Rule
evidence.supports: Indirect rule, invented chieftaincy and labour migration across British West Africa.

contested.note: How far Britain deliberately underdeveloped the north, as against simply not spending on a territory with no export crop, is argued about. The policy documents show both: an explicit labour-reserve doctrine, and a Treasury unwilling to fund anything.

pedagogy.hook: The first secondary school in northern Ghana opened in 1951, forty-nine years after Britain declared the protectorate and seventy-six years after the first one on the coast.

misconception.belief: Colonial rule brought schools, hospitals and roads to Africa.
misconception.correction: It brought them where they paid. The Gold Coast's cocoa-growing south got railways, harbours, secondary schools and a university college. The Northern Territories, with no export crop, got a policy of supplying labour to the south and almost no schools at all. The gap between them is still the sharpest inequality in Ghana.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The uneven map inside a single colony explains more about post-independence African politics than the borders between colonies do. Ghana inherited a north-south divide that Britain designed.

keyDates.what: George Ekem Ferguson, Britain's treaty-maker in the north, is killed at Wa
The Northern Territories protectorate takes effect
The Talensi are finally subdued in the Tongo hills
The first northern secondary school opens at Tamale
Independence inside Ghana

territories.name: British Togoland
territories.formalName: The Trust Territory of Togoland under United Kingdom administration
territories.subregion: Western third of former German Togoland

namesOverTime.name: Togoland
namesOverTime.note: Germany's protectorate, taken by treaty with Mlapa III at Togoville in July 1884.

namesOverTime.name: Trans-Volta Togoland
namesOverTime.note: The name of the Ghanaian region before it became the Volta Region.

namesOverTime.name: The Volta and Oti regions of Ghana
namesOverTime.note: The Ewe south of the territory voted against union and was joined to Ghana anyway; the Ewe unification claim has never gone away.

modernSuccessors.name: Ghana
modernSuccessors.note: Ghana's Volta and Oti regions. A Togoland separatist movement has existed on and off ever since; there were arrests over declarations of a 'Western Togoland' as recently as 2019-20.

geoCoverage.label: All of German Togoland under Anglo-French occupation
geoCoverage.change: German Togoland surrendered after three weeks — the first German colony to fall in the First World War — and Britain and France occupied it jointly.

geoCoverage.label: The western third only
geoCoverage.change: Britain and France partitioned the occupied colony: France took the east with the capital at Lomé, Britain took a western strip about a third of the territory and administered it as if it were part of the Gold Coast.

acquisitions.how: British troops from the Gold Coast and French troops from Dahomey invaded German Togoland on 6 August 1914; the Germans blew up their new wireless station at Kamina and surrendered on 26 August.

counterparties.name: The German Empire
counterparties.lost: Germany lost its first colony of the war, three weeks after it began, along with the wireless mast that linked Berlin to its ships in the South Atlantic.

counterparties.name: The Ewe, Dagomba, Konkomba and Kabye peoples of Togoland
counterparties.lost: They exchanged one European ruler for two, and within two years found a new international border running through their towns and families.

people.name: Frederick Bryant
people.role: commanded the Gold Coast Regiment force that invaded Togoland

people.name: Hans-Georg von Doering
people.role: acting German governor who surrendered the colony

acquisitions.resistance: The German force was mostly African police and reservists; the campaign cost a few hundred casualties on all sides and was over in twenty days.

acquisitions.how: The League of Nations confirmed Britain's mandate over western Togoland, with an obligation to report annually and, in theory, to prepare the territory for self-rule.

counterparties.name: The German Empire
counterparties.lost: Germany lost all its colonies at Versailles on the argument that it was unfit to govern them, and the territories were distributed among the victors as mandates.

counterparties.name: The Ewe people
counterparties.lost: The Ewe were now divided three ways: between the Gold Coast Colony, British Togoland and French Togoland. Reuniting them became the central political demand of the region for the next forty years.

instrument.name: League of Nations Mandate for Togoland (British)
instrument.note: The provisional Anglo-French partition of 1916 was confirmed with adjustments in 1919 and given legal form as a mandate in 1922.

acquisitions.how: The United Nations turned the mandate into a trusteeship, with visiting missions, a right of petition and an obligation to consult the inhabitants about their future — which is what forced the 1956 plebiscite.

counterparties.name: The people of British Togoland
counterparties.lost: Nothing was lost at this step, and something was gained: for the first time the inhabitants could petition an international body over Britain's head, and thousands of them did.

instrument.name: Trusteeship Agreement for Togoland under United Kingdom administration

statusPeriods.label: Military occupation and provisional partition
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British and French officers divided the German colony between them in 1916 by agreement, drawing a line that cut Ewe country in two and did not follow any earlier boundary.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Accra

statusPeriods.label: League of Nations mandate, run from Accra
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain administered the mandate as though it were part of the Gold Coast — same governor, same officials, same courts — while filing annual reports to Geneva about a territory it was supposed to be preparing for self-rule.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Accra, with reports to the Permanent Mandates Commission in Geneva
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. Togolanders had no representation of their own; the northern section was administered with the Northern Territories and the south with the Gold Coast Colony.

statusPeriods.label: UN trust territory
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Administration did not change, but the United Nations now sent visiting missions, received petitions from Ewe unification groups and eventually required Britain to hold a plebiscite before the trusteeship could end.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Accra, under UN Trusteeship Council supervision
statusPeriods.franchise: Togolanders voted in Gold Coast elections from 1951 and in the plebiscite of 9 May 1956.
statusPeriods.note: The All-Ewe Conference and the Togoland Congress sent petition after petition to the UN asking for Ewe reunification. They got a plebiscite with only two options, neither of which was reunification.

departures.how: In a UN-supervised plebiscite on 9 May 1956 about 58 per cent voted to join the Gold Coast; the north voted heavily for union and the Ewe south heavily against, and the whole territory joined Ghana on independence day.

led.name: Sylvanus Olympio
led.role: leader of Ewe unification politics and later first President of independent Togo; assassinated in 1963

led.name: S.G. Antor
led.role: leader of the Togoland Congress, which campaigned against union with the Gold Coast and boycotted parts of the process

led.name: Kwame Nkrumah
led.role: campaigned for union and won the southern vote in the northern section

departures.movement: Togoland Congress (against union); Convention People's Party (for union)

cost.note: The plebiscite itself was peaceful. There were clashes in Ewe districts in 1956-57 and arrests afterwards; no reliable death toll was compiled, and it was small.

departures.borders: The 1916 Anglo-French line became the Ghana-Togo border. It cuts Ewe country in half, and the plebiscite offered no option to reunite it: the choice was union with the Gold Coast or continued trusteeship, never reunification with French Togoland.

instrument.name: UN General Assembly Resolution 1044 (XI) approving the union of British Togoland with the Gold Coast
instrument.note: The union took legal effect when the Gold Coast became independent on 6 March 1957 and the trusteeship ended.

contested.note: The plebiscite is disputed to this day: the ballot excluded reunification with French Togoland, the two sections voted in opposite directions, and the result was applied to the whole territory rather than section by section. Ghana's Volta region has produced separatist movements ever since.

evidence.author: D.E.K. Amenumey
evidence.work: The Ewe Unification Movement: A Political History
evidence.supports: The Ewe unification campaign, the petitions to the UN and the 1956 plebiscite.

partition.note: German Togoland was partitioned twice: between Britain and France in 1916, and again in 1956-57 when British Togoland went to Ghana and French Togoland became Togo.
partition.lineDrawnBy: British and French colonial officials, provisionally in December 1916 and confirmed in 1919

consequences.borderLegacy: The Ghana-Togo border is a First World War military convenience. Ewe families, markets and chieftaincies straddle it, and the smuggling economy along it is a century old.

commonwealth.note: As part of Ghana. Togo, the French half, joined the Commonwealth in its own right in 2022 — a country Britain ruled for two years and France for forty.

consequences.languageAndLaw: Ghana's Volta region speaks Ewe and works in English; across the border the same people speak Ewe and work in French.

peak.populationNote: The 1948 census of British Togoland counted a little over 380,000 people. The drawn shape in this atlas is approximate: the geometry team could not reconstruct the 1956 plebiscite boundary, so the mapped area is larger than the real 33,775 km².

evidence.author: D.E.K. Amenumey
evidence.work: The Ewe Unification Movement: A Political History
evidence.supports: Ewe politics, the UN petitions and the plebiscite.

evidence.author: Dennis Austin
evidence.work: Politics in Ghana, 1946-1960
evidence.supports: The plebiscite campaign and its place in Gold Coast politics.

contested.note: The legitimacy of the 1956 plebiscite is genuinely disputed. Supporters point to a UN-supervised majority; critics point to a ballot with no reunification option, to opposite results in the two sections, and to a whole-territory result imposed on a section that voted the other way.

pedagogy.hook: British Togoland is the only part of the British Empire that voted itself out of existence — and the half that voted no was outvoted by the half that voted yes.

misconception.belief: Mandates and trust territories were a fairer, more temporary kind of colony.
misconception.correction: Britain administered Togoland as if it were part of the Gold Coast for 41 years: same governor, same officials, same laws. What the mandate and trusteeship actually changed was the paperwork — annual reports to Geneva, then visiting missions and a right of petition to New York. That right of petition mattered: it is the reason a plebiscite happened at all.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows what self-determination looked like when the options were written by other people. Togolanders were asked a question with two answers, and the answer they most wanted — reunite the Ewe — was not on the paper.

keyDates.what: Germany declares a protectorate over Togoland
Togoland surrenders: the first German colony to fall in the war
Britain and France partition it, cutting Ewe country in two
League of Nations mandate confirmed
Plebiscite: about 58 per cent vote to join the Gold Coast

territories.name: Lagos
territories.formalName: The Colony of Lagos

namesOverTime.name: Eko

from.note: A rough marker for the pre-contact period, not an event.

namesOverTime.note: The Yoruba name, from the Bini word for a war camp; still the everyday name of the city.

namesOverTime.name: Lagos

from.note: A rough marker for when Portuguese usage settled, not an event.

namesOverTime.note: 'Lakes', for the lagoon.

namesOverTime.name: The Colony (of Nigeria)
namesOverTime.note: Lagos remained legally 'the Colony' — the only part of Nigeria under British sovereignty. Everything else was protectorate.

modernSuccessors.name: Nigeria
modernSuccessors.note: Lagos was Nigeria's capital until 1991, when the federal government moved to Abuja. It is now one of the largest cities on earth.

geoCoverage.label: A consulate and a gunboat
geoCoverage.change: After bombarding Lagos in December 1851 and installing a king who would sign an anti-slave-trade treaty, Britain put a consul on the island and governed nothing.

geoCoverage.label: The Colony of Lagos
geoCoverage.change: The Oba ceded the island under the guns of HMS Prometheus; the colony later spread along the lagoon and mainland but stayed small.

acquisitions.how: Royal Navy ships shelled Lagos over three days in December 1851, drove out Oba Kosoko, installed his rival Akitoye, and left a consul behind to hold the new king to a treaty against the slave trade.

counterparties.name: The kingdom of Lagos
counterparties.lost: Lagos lost the right to choose its own Oba. Kosoko was removed by foreign gunfire and Akitoye ruled on British terms, which is a loss of sovereignty however it is described.

instrument.name: Treaty between Great Britain and Lagos for the abolition of the slave trade

people.name: Kosoko
people.role: Oba of Lagos, driven out by the 1851 bombardment; returned to Lagos in 1862 and lived there until 1872

people.name: Akitoye
people.role: Oba installed by Britain in 1851 in place of his nephew

people.name: John Beecroft
people.role: British consul for the Bights of Benin and Biafra, who pushed the attack

acquisitions.resistance: Kosoko's men fought the first British landing off in November 1851 and inflicted real casualties; the second attack, in December with heavier ships, took the town.

cost.note: British casualties in the December 1851 attack ran to a few dozen killed and wounded. Lagos casualties were far higher and were never counted; much of the town burned.

evidence.author: Robert Smith
evidence.work: The Lagos Consulate 1851-1861
evidence.supports: The bombardment, the consulate and the road to annexation.

acquisitions.how: Oba Dosunmu signed away Lagos to Queen Victoria aboard a British warship after being told that if he refused, the guns of HMS Prometheus, already trained on his palace, would open fire.

counterparties.name: The kingdom of Lagos
counterparties.lost: Dosunmu lost his kingdom and kept his title and a pension of about £1,030 a year, paid in cowries. The Oba of Lagos has been a ceremonial ruler ever since.

instrument.name: Lagos Treaty of Cession
instrument.note: Signed under duress: the British commander had made clear that the alternative was bombardment. Dosunmu protested the terms afterwards and was ignored.

people.name: Dosunmu
people.role: Oba of Lagos who signed the cession under the threat of bombardment

people.name: William McCoskry
people.role: acting consul who negotiated the cession

people.name: Norman Bedingfield
people.role: commander of HMS Prometheus, whose guns supplied the argument

acquisitions.resistance: Dosunmu signed rather than see the town shelled a second time in ten years. His protests to London about the terms went nowhere.

evidence.author: Kristin Mann
evidence.work: Slavery and the Birth of an African City: Lagos, 1760-1900
evidence.supports: The cession, Lagos society and the transition from slave trading to palm oil.

statusPeriods.label: Consulate under the guns
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British consul with no legal authority over anyone advised a king Britain had installed, backed by warships that had already destroyed the town once.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: the consulate at Lagos, under the Foreign Office
statusPeriods.note: This is what 'informal empire' looked like on the West African coast, and it lasted nine years before Britain gave up pretending and annexed the place.

statusPeriods.label: The Colony: British soil in Nigeria
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Lagos was British sovereign territory, so people born there were British subjects with British passports; a governor ruled with a nominated council, and from 1923 a handful of elected seats.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Lagos, under Freetown 1866-74, Accra 1874-86, its own governor 1886-1906, and then Nigeria
statusPeriods.franchise: The 1922 Clifford constitution gave Lagos three elected seats — the first elective franchise anywhere in British Africa — restricted to men with an income of £100 a year. Perhaps a few thousand people qualified.
statusPeriods.note: Lagos was passed between administrations five times: West African Settlements from 1866, the Gold Coast from 1874, its own colony from 1886, Southern Nigeria from 1906, Nigeria from 1914, and Federal Territory from 1954.

departures.how: The one piece of Nigeria that was legally British soil became the capital of an independent federation, and its people stopped being British subjects overnight.

led.name: Herbert Macaulay
led.role: engineer and journalist, grandson of Bishop Samuel Ajayi Crowther; founded the Nigerian National Democratic Party in 1923 and won the first African elections in British Africa

led.name: Nnamdi Azikiwe
led.role: newspaper proprietor and politician; co-founded the NCNC with Macaulay in 1944 and became Nigeria's first Governor-General

departures.movement: Nigerian National Democratic Party, then the NCNC

cost.note: Nobody died at independence in Lagos. The city's costs were paid in 1851, when the Royal Navy burned much of it, and after 1966, when it was the capital of a state at war with itself.

departures.borders: Lagos ceased to be a separate legal entity and became the Federal Territory of an independent Nigeria; the colony-protectorate distinction that had made its people British subjects disappeared with the empire.

slavery.note: Britain took Lagos to stop the slave trade and then built a palm-oil economy on the labour of people who were still enslaved inside Yorubaland for another fifty years.

abolitionDate.note: The treaty Britain imposed after the bombardment. Slave exports from Lagos did not stop immediately.

emancipationDate.note: Slavery was abolished in the Colony of Lagos itself; it remained legal in the protectorates around it for decades.

populationTransfer.note: Thousands of Saro — Yoruba recaptives freed at Freetown — and Amaro returnees from Brazil and Cuba settled in Lagos and became its merchant and professional class.

consequences.economicLegacy: Lagos went from a slave-trading port to a palm-oil port to the commercial capital of Africa's largest economy; its harbour was dredged with colonial loans that Nigerian revenue repaid.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English common law, an elected municipal politics dating from 1923, and a Nigerian press founded in Lagos that trained the generation who took power in 1960.

peak.populationNote: 1952-53 census figure for Lagos town. The 1866 estimate was about 25,000.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Lagos’s largest recorded population: 267,407 people, counted in 1952.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Kristin Mann
evidence.work: Slavery and the Birth of an African City: Lagos, 1760-1900
evidence.supports: Lagos society, slavery and the transformation of the city under British rule.

evidence.author: Robert Smith
evidence.work: The Lagos Consulate 1851-1861
evidence.supports: The bombardment, the consulate and the 1861 cession.

evidence.author: Toyin Falola and Matthew M. Heaton
evidence.work: A History of Nigeria
evidence.supports: Lagos in the wider Nigerian story to 1960.

pedagogy.hook: The Oba of Lagos signed his kingdom away in 1861 on a British warship whose guns were already pointed at his palace.

misconception.belief: Britain took over Lagos to stop the slave trade there, so this bit of empire was at least well intentioned.
misconception.correction: The slave trade was the stated reason and it was real: Lagos was a major exporting port. But Britain kept the place, made it a colony, built a customs house and taxed the palm-oil trade that replaced slaving. A humanitarian argument opened the door and a commercial interest walked through it. Both halves of that sentence are documented in the same despatches.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Lagos was the seed of Nigeria. Everything Britain later added — the delta, the Niger company's territories, Yorubaland, Benin, the Sokoto Caliphate — was administered outward from this one island it took in 1861.

keyDates.what: The Royal Navy bombards Lagos and installs a new Oba
Oba Dosunmu cedes Lagos under threat of bombardment
Lagos merged into Southern Nigeria
Lagos elects three members: the first African elections in the British Empire in Africa
Capital of independent Nigeria

territories.name: Nigeria
territories.formalName: The Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria
territories.subregion: Niger and Benue basins and the Bight of Biafra

namesOverTime.name: Nigeria
namesOverTime.note: Coined by the journalist Flora Shaw in a Times article, as a tidier alternative to 'the Royal Niger Company Territories'. She later married Frederick Lugard, who governed the country she had named.

modernSuccessors.name: Nigeria
modernSuccessors.note: A republic since 1 October 1963, and the most populous country in Africa. British Northern Cameroons joined it on 1 June 1961.

geoCoverage.label: One island colony
geoCoverage.change: Britain held Lagos and nothing else; the palm-oil trade of the delta ran through consuls and gunboats, not government.

geoCoverage.label: Lagos and the Oil Rivers
geoCoverage.change: Four months after the Berlin Conference closed, Britain proclaimed a protectorate over the Niger delta to register a claim before France and Germany did.

geoCoverage.label: A colony, a protectorate and a chartered company
geoCoverage.change: The Royal Niger Company's charter let a London company claim the Niger and Benue basins; most of what it claimed it had never seen, let alone governed.

geoCoverage.label: One Nigeria
geoCoverage.change: Lugard amalgamated Northern and Southern Nigeria into a single Colony and Protectorate, mainly so that southern customs revenue could pay for the northern administration.

acquisitions.how: Oba Dosunmu ceded Lagos aboard a British warship with its guns trained on his palace, giving Britain its first sovereign foothold in what became Nigeria.

counterparties.name: The kingdom of Lagos
counterparties.lost: Its independence, its customs revenue and the right to choose its own Oba.

acquisitions.how: Britain declared a protectorate over the Niger delta on the strength of treaties its consuls had collected from delta rulers, to satisfy the Berlin Conference's rule that a claim had to be notified and occupied.

counterparties.name: The delta city-states: Bonny, Opobo, Brass, Old Calabar, Nembe and Itsekiri Warri
counterparties.lost: They lost the middleman position that had made them rich for two centuries: their whole business was buying palm oil inland and selling it to Europeans on the coast, and Britain wanted the Europeans to buy inland directly.

people.name: Jaja of Opobo
people.role: born enslaved in Igbo country, became king of Opobo and the delta's most successful trader; tricked aboard a British warship in 1887, tried and exiled to St Vincent

people.name: Harry Johnston
people.role: acting consul who lured Jaja aboard HMS Goshawk under a promise of safe conduct and deported him

acquisitions.resistance: Jaja of Opobo blockaded British firms out of his rivers and was removed by trickery; Nana Olomu of the Itsekiri was attacked and deported in 1894; the Nembe under King Koko sacked the Royal Niger Company's base at Akassa in January 1895 and were bombarded for it.

evidence.author: Martin Lynn
evidence.work: Commerce and Economic Change in West Africa: The Palm Oil Trade in the Nineteenth Century
evidence.supports: The delta middlemen, the palm-oil trade and the conflicts that ended it.

acquisitions.how: The Crown gave George Goldie's company a charter to govern, tax and police the Niger and Benue basins, so that Britain could claim the territory at Berlin without paying for an administration.

counterparties.name: The Sokoto Caliphate and the emirates of Nupe, Ilorin and Kontagora
counterparties.lost: The company presented treaties signed by rulers who understood them as trade agreements as if they were cessions of sovereignty, and used them to claim their territory in European law.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Nikki and the states of Borgu
counterparties.lost: Britain and France both claimed Borgu on the strength of rival treaties in 1894-98 and nearly went to war over it; Borgu was divided between them without being consulted.

instrument.name: Royal Charter of the Royal Niger Company
instrument.note: The charter was revoked on 1 January 1900 and the Crown paid the company £865,000 for its assets and rights, plus a share of mineral royalties for 99 years.

people.name: George Taubman Goldie
people.role: built the company that became the Royal Niger Company and used it to claim Nigeria for Britain on the cheap

acquisitions.resistance: The Nembe of Brass, ruined by the company's trade monopoly, attacked and burned its headquarters at Akassa in January 1895; a British punitive expedition destroyed Nembe town in reply.

evidence.author: Toyin Falola and Matthew M. Heaton
evidence.work: A History of Nigeria
evidence.supports: The Royal Niger Company, its charter and its revocation.

acquisitions.how: A punitive expedition of about 1,200 men took Benin City, burned it, deposed the Oba and shipped several thousand brass plaques, ivories and carvings to London to be auctioned to pay for the operation.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Benin
counterparties.lost: A kingdom some six centuries old lost its capital, its independence, its Oba and the royal art of its whole history, which is now in about 160 museums in Europe and North America.

acquisitions.how: Lugard's West African Frontier Force took Kano in February and Sokoto in March 1903 with machine guns against cavalry, ending the largest independent state in Africa and installing a new Sultan the same week.

counterparties.name: The Sokoto Caliphate
counterparties.lost: A state of perhaps ten to fifteen million people, founded in a jihad in 1804 and covering most of what is now northern Nigeria, lost its independence in eight weeks of fighting.

acquisitions.resistance: Sultan Attahiru I refused to submit, left Sokoto with thousands of followers on a religious migration eastward, and was killed with hundreds of them at Burmi on 27 July 1903.

statusPeriods.label: The Colony of Lagos alone
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A governor at Lagos ruled one island and a strip of lagoon shore, and dealt with the Yoruba states inland as foreign powers, mediating their wars.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Lagos, under Freetown or Accra at different dates

statusPeriods.label: Colony plus the Oil Rivers Protectorate
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Consuls with warships behind them told delta kings what trade they could do, and deposed the ones who refused.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: the consulate at Calabar, under the Foreign Office

statusPeriods.label: A colony, a protectorate and a company with an army
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Three different Britains governed at once: a Crown colony at Lagos, a Foreign Office protectorate in the delta, and the Royal Niger Company, which levied its own customs, ran its own courts and fought its own wars up the Niger.
statusPeriods.controlDegreeNote: The default 4 fits the company's legal powers but not its reach: the Royal Niger Company had a few hundred soldiers, a river fleet and treaties, and it administered almost none of the territory it claimed.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Lagos, Calabar and the company's headquarters at Asaba
statusPeriods.note: The company's constabulary was about 400 men. On that basis Britain claimed a territory larger than France.

statusPeriods.label: Two protectorates and a colony
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Crown revoked the charter, paid the company off, and split its territory into the Protectorates of Northern and Southern Nigeria, which then spent fourteen years conquering the places the company had only claimed on paper.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Zungeru for the north, Calabar then Lagos for the south, under the Colonial Office

statusPeriods.label: One Nigeria under indirect rule
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: About 400 British administrators governed twenty million people through emirs, obas and, where no chief existed, through 'warrant chiefs' they appointed themselves — the doctrine Lugard wrote up as indirect rule.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Lagos, under the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.franchise: Three elected Lagos seats and one for Calabar from 1923, on a £100 income qualification. The Richards constitution of 1946 brought regional councils, the Macpherson constitution of 1951 a national assembly, and the Lyttelton constitution of 1954 a federation.
statusPeriods.note: Indirect rule meant something different in each region: real emirs in the north, real obas in the west, and in the Igbo east chiefs invented by British officers for societies that had governed themselves by assembly. That invention caused the Aba Women's War of 1929.

statusPeriods.label: Federal self-government under Balewa
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Abubakar Tafawa Balewa led a federal government of Nigerian ministers; the Western and Eastern Regions took internal self-government in 1957 and the Northern Region in March 1959, each at its own pace.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Lagos
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage in the south; in the Northern Region women could not vote in federal elections until 1976.

departures.how: After three constitutional conferences and staggered regional self-government, Britain handed over a federation of three unequal regions to Abubakar Tafawa Balewa's government without a shot being fired.

led.name: Abubakar Tafawa Balewa
led.role: teacher from Bauchi, first and only Prime Minister of the First Republic; killed in the coup of January 1966

led.name: Nnamdi Azikiwe
led.role: founded the West African Pilot in 1937, led the NCNC, first Governor-General and then President

led.name: Obafemi Awolowo
led.role: founded the Action Group and the Western Region's free primary education scheme; leader of the opposition, later jailed for treasonable felony

led.name: Ahmadu Bello
led.role: Sardauna of Sokoto, Premier of the Northern Region and the real power in the federation; killed in January 1966

led.name: Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti
led.role: led the Abeokuta Women's Union, forced the Alake to abdicate in 1949 over taxation of women, and campaigned for women's suffrage

departures.movement: NCNC, Action Group and the Northern People's Congress

cost.note: Nobody died at independence. The bill came later: the January and July coups of 1966, massacres of Igbo people in the north that killed something in the range of 8,000 to 30,000, and a civil war from 1967 to 1970 whose death toll is estimated between 500,000 and three million, most of them children who starved under blockade.

departures.borders: Nigeria's borders were fixed by Anglo-French and Anglo-German conventions between 1890 and 1913. Inside them Britain left a federation of three regions in which the Northern Region alone held more than half the seats — a structure that made the census a weapon and the constitution a permanent argument.

instrument.name: Nigeria Independence Act 1960
instrument.note: Royal assent July 1960; independence took effect on 1 October 1960.

evidence.author: Toyin Falola and Matthew M. Heaton
evidence.work: A History of Nigeria
evidence.supports: The constitutional conferences, regionalism and the handover.

violence.note: Britain conquered Nigeria piece by piece over forty years, from the Benin expedition of 1897 to the last Middle Belt campaigns of the 1920s, and shot fifty-one women dead at Opobo in 1929 for protesting about taxation.

toll.note: Deaths in the Aba Women's War of November-December 1929, as counted by the two British commissions of inquiry that followed it. Roughly the same number were wounded. Nobody counted the dead of the conquest campaigns.

warrant.author: The Aba Commission of Inquiry
warrant.work: Report of the Commission of Inquiry into the Disturbances in the Calabar and Owerri Provinces, December 1929
warrant.supports: Deaths in the Aba Women's War of November-December 1929, as counted by the two British commissions of inquiry that followed it. Roughly the same number were wounded. Nobody counted the dead of the conquest campaigns.
warrant.check: Reports of colonial commissions and boards of inquiry are Command Papers: British Parliamentary Papers, and the CO series at The National Archives, Kew.
warrant.note: A figure exists for Aba because the killings embarrassed the administration into an inquiry. No inquiry followed the conquest patrols, and no figure exists for those.

slavery.note: Nigeria's coast supplied the Bight of Biafra trade, from which roughly 1.6 million people were shipped, most of them Igbo and Ibibio and most of them in British ships.

emancipationDate.note: The legal status of slavery in Northern Nigeria was abolished in 1901 but mass emancipation was deliberately prevented; slavery was only fully outlawed there in 1936, the last such measure in the British Empire.

toll.note: Bight of Biafra embarkation totals come from the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database and are reconstructions from surviving voyage records.

commonwealth.note: A republic since 1963. Nigeria was suspended from the Commonwealth in 1995 after the execution of Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other Ogoni activists, and readmitted in 1999.

consequences.borderLegacy: Nigeria's external borders were agreed between Europeans in the 1890s and split Hausa, Kanuri, Yoruba and Ejagham communities with Niger, Benin, Chad and Cameroon. The internal border that mattered most was the one Britain drew in 1914 between North and South.
consequences.economicLegacy: Palm oil, then groundnuts and cocoa, then oil. The Niger delta oilfields were opened by Shell-BP under a colonial concession granted in 1938 that covered the whole country.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English is the official language of a country with over 500 of them; the north runs sharia courts beside English common law, an arrangement Lugard's indirect rule created and independence inherited.

peak.populationNote: The 1952-53 census, the last reliable colonial count. The 1962 and 1963 censuses were inflated for political advantage — seats and revenue depended on them — and the 1963 total of 55.6 million is not trusted by demographers.

populationWarrant.author: The government that took the census
populationWarrant.supports: Nigeria’s largest recorded population: 30,403,302 people, counted in 1952.
populationWarrant.check: Colonial census returns are printed in the territory’s own census report and in its annual Blue Book or administration report; the British copies are in the CO, IOR and FO series at The National Archives, Kew, and in the India Office Records at the British Library.
populationWarrant.note: A colonial census counted what the administration wanted counted and reached where its officers reached. Undercounts of rural, pastoral and colonised populations were normal, and several of these returns say so themselves.

evidence.author: Toyin Falola and Matthew M. Heaton
evidence.work: A History of Nigeria
evidence.supports: The whole arc from the delta trade to independence and the civil war.

evidence.author: Frederick Lugard
evidence.work: The Dual Mandate in British Tropical Africa
evidence.supports: Indirect rule as its architect explained and justified it.

evidence.author: Michael Crowder
evidence.work: The Story of Nigeria
evidence.supports: The conquest, amalgamation and administration of Nigeria.

contested.note: The 1914 amalgamation is argued about in Nigeria to this day: whether it created a viable country or forced together a Muslim north and a Christian south for the convenience of British accounting. Historians also disagree about the civil war death toll, where estimates run from 500,000 to three million.

pedagogy.hook: Nigeria's name was invented by a journalist in a newspaper article in 1897, and she later married the man who governed it.

misconception.belief: Britain united Nigeria and gave it a national government.
misconception.correction: Lugard amalgamated North and South on 1 January 1914 for a reason he stated plainly: southern customs revenue could subsidise the northern administration. The two halves kept separate legal systems, separate school policies and separate civil services, and Britain kept Christian missions out of the Muslim north. Nigeria was joined on the ledger and kept apart on the ground.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Nigeria is the biggest thing Britain built in Africa and the clearest case of what indirect rule cost. The federation of 1954, the regional imbalance, the census wars and the civil war of 1967-70 all run back to decisions taken in Lagos and London between 1900 and 1914.

The Royal Niger Company chartered to govern the Niger basin
Charter revoked; the Crown pays £865,000 and takes over
Sokoto falls; the largest state in Africa is conquered

territories.name: Southern Nigeria
territories.formalName: The Colony and Protectorate of Southern Nigeria
territories.subregion: Niger delta, Igbo and Yoruba country

namesOverTime.name: Consulate of the Bights of Benin and Biafra
namesOverTime.note: A consul with no territory, based on Spanish Fernando Po, whose authority rested on the Royal Navy squadron.

namesOverTime.name: Oil Rivers Protectorate
namesOverTime.note: The 'oil' was palm oil, not petroleum — a coincidence that has confused students for a century.

namesOverTime.name: The Southern Provinces, then the Western and Eastern Regions
namesOverTime.note: Split into Western and Eastern Provinces in 1939 and made self-governing Regions in 1957.

namesOverTime.name: Southern Nigeria
namesOverTime.language: English, Yoruba, Igbo, Efik and others
namesOverTime.note: No longer an administrative unit: the ground is now seventeen states of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, in the three southern geopolitical zones.

modernSuccessors.name: Nigeria
modernSuccessors.note: The Eastern Region seceded as Biafra in 1967 and was reconquered by 1970.

geoCoverage.label: Consular influence on the rivers only
geoCoverage.change: A consul and a naval squadron dealt with delta kings; Britain governed nobody and claimed nothing.

geoCoverage.label: Protectorate on paper, conquest in progress
geoCoverage.change: The protectorate was proclaimed in 1885 and then had to be made real: the Benin expedition in 1897, the Aro expedition in 1901-02 and a decade of patrols through Igbo country.

geoCoverage.label: The Southern Provinces of Nigeria
geoCoverage.change: Amalgamated with the north into one Nigeria, and administered as the Southern Provinces and later as the Western and Eastern Regions.

acquisitions.how: Britain appointed John Beecroft consul for the Bights of Benin and Biafra, a man who was simultaneously the Spanish governor of Fernando Po, and gave him warships to enforce anti-slave-trade treaties on kings he had no authority over.

counterparties.name: The delta city-states and the Efik of Old Calabar
counterparties.lost: They kept their thrones and lost the ability to refuse. Consuls deposed kings, arbitrated successions and fixed trade terms, and behind every request was a gunboat.

people.name: John Beecroft
people.role: British consul for the Bights and, at the same time, Spanish governor of Fernando Po; the single most powerful European on this coast in the 1850s

acquisitions.how: Britain proclaimed the Oil Rivers Protectorate over the delta, four months after the Berlin Conference ruled that European claims had to be notified and backed by effective occupation.

counterparties.name: Bonny, Opobo, Nembe, Old Calabar and the Itsekiri of Warri
counterparties.lost: The delta states had been the middlemen of the palm-oil trade for generations. Britain's aim was to remove them so that British firms could buy directly upriver, and within a decade Jaja of Opobo and Nana Olomu had both been deported.

acquisitions.resistance: Jaja blockaded the rivers; Nana Olomu fought a naval expedition at Ebrohimi in 1894; King Koko of Nembe sacked the Royal Niger Company's depot at Akassa in January 1895 and his town was destroyed in reprisal.

evidence.author: Martin Lynn
evidence.work: Commerce and Economic Change in West Africa: The Palm Oil Trade in the Nineteenth Century

pedagogy.hook: The largest independent state in Africa in 1900 was conquered in eight weeks, and its conqueror kept the same rulers in the same palaces for the next sixty years.

misconception.belief: Pre-colonial Africa had no states, no writing and no bureaucracy.
