cost.note: Nine of ten Britons in the January 1897 Phillips party were killed, along with most of the roughly 220 African carriers with them. Benin's own dead in February were never counted; the city burned for days.

evidence.author: Dan Hicks
evidence.work: The Brutish Museums: The Benin Bronzes, Colonial Violence and Cultural Restitution
evidence.supports: The expedition, the looting, the dispersal of the objects and the restitution argument.

statusPeriods.label: The kingdom abolished, the Oba exiled
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: With the Oba deported, British officers ruled through a council of Benin chiefs they selected, and the throne stood empty for seventeen years.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Benin City, under the Niger Coast and then Southern Nigeria protectorate
statusPeriods.note: Ovonramwen was tried at Benin City in September 1897 by the men who had just destroyed his capital, and exiled to Calabar. He never returned.

statusPeriods.label: The Oba restored as a Native Authority
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain restored Ovonramwen's son as Oba Eweka II and made him a Native Authority under indirect rule: the throne came back with a British Resident attached to it.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Benin City, under the Southern Provinces of Nigeria
statusPeriods.note: Restoring the monarchy was cheaper than replacing it. Benin's brass casters, whose guild had worked for the Oba for five centuries, resumed work for a court with no power.

departures.how: Benin became part of independent Nigeria with its Oba still on the throne and its royal art still in London, Berlin, Vienna, New York and about 160 other collections.

led.name: Akenzua II
led.role: Oba of Benin from 1933; campaigned for a Mid-West Region and for the return of Benin's looted art

led.name: Nnamdi Azikiwe
led.role: led the NCNC, the party that carried the Benin area at independence

departures.movement: NCNC, and the Mid-West movement that created a separate region in 1963

cost.note: Nobody died in 1960. Benin's cost was paid in February 1897, and it is still being argued over in museum committee rooms.

departures.borders: Benin's territory became part of Nigeria's Western Region and then, from 1963, the Mid-Western Region — the only new region created in the First Republic.

violence.note: Benin City was stormed, looted and burned in February 1897, and its Oba was tried by the officers who had destroyed it.

populationTransfer.note: Britain also removed Benin's objects: perhaps 3,000 to 5,000 brasses, ivories and carvings left in 1897 and were sold to museums and collectors across Europe and America.

consequences.economicLegacy: The expedition was financed by selling the loot. The Foreign Office kept a share of the objects to defray costs, and the British Museum received several hundred plaques.
consequences.languageAndLaw: The Oba of Benin, restored by the British in 1914 as an instrument of indirect rule, remains one of the most respected traditional institutions in Nigeria.

peak.populationNote: No reliable population figure exists for the kingdom before 1897. Seventeenth-century Dutch visitors described a walled city with broad straight streets larger than any they knew in the Netherlands.

evidence.author: Dan Hicks
evidence.work: The Brutish Museums: The Benin Bronzes, Colonial Violence and Cultural Restitution
evidence.supports: The 1897 expedition, the scale of the looting and the restitution debate.

evidence.author: Robert Home
evidence.work: City of Blood Revisited: A New Look at the Benin Expedition of 1897
evidence.supports: The military course of the expedition and the propaganda that justified it.

evidence.author: Toyin Falola and Matthew M. Heaton
evidence.work: A History of Nigeria
evidence.supports: Benin's place in the making of Southern Nigeria.

contested.note: Two things are argued about. First, whether the January 1897 ambush was a trap or a blunder by Phillips, who marched on the city during a festival after being told to stay away. Second, where the objects should be now: Nigeria's federal government, the Oba of Benin and Edo State have all claimed custody of returned pieces.

pedagogy.hook: Britain paid for the expedition that destroyed Benin by auctioning the art it stole from Benin.

misconception.belief: West African societies had no fine art before Europeans arrived; the Benin Bronzes must be later or European-influenced.
misconception.correction: The brasses were cast by Benin's own guild using the lost-wax method from at least the fifteenth century, and their quality astonished Europeans in 1897 so much that some German scholars insisted Africans could not have made them. The metal came from European trade, the skill and the tradition did not. The Vienna and Berlin museums have since accepted this and begun returning pieces.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Benin Bronzes are the most argued-about objects in any museum. Knowing exactly how they left Benin — a punitive expedition, a burned city, an auction to cover costs — is what makes the restitution argument a question about evidence rather than taste.

keyDates.what: Phillips's party is ambushed on the road to Benin
Benin City stormed, burned and looted
Oba Ovonramwen tried and exiled to Calabar
Britain restores his son Eweka II as a Native Authority
Germany transfers ownership of over a thousand Benin objects to Nigeria

territories.name: Egba United Government
territories.formalName: The Egba United Government at Abeokuta

namesOverTime.name: Abeokuta
namesOverTime.note: 'Under the rock'. Founded about 1830 by Egba refugees from the wars that followed the collapse of the Oyo empire.

namesOverTime.name: Egba United Board of Management
namesOverTime.note: An administration set up by returned Saro — Yoruba freed at Freetown and educated there — with a treasury, a customs service and a printing press.

modernSuccessors.name: Nigeria
modernSuccessors.note: Abeokuta is the capital of Ogun State.

geoCoverage.label: Egbaland around Abeokuta
geoCoverage.change: No geo unit exists at this scale; the map hatches Southern Nigeria and marks Abeokuta with a point.

acquisitions.how: Governor Gilbert Carter signed a treaty at Abeokuta that guaranteed Egba independence in exchange for free trade and open roads, making Britain the guarantor of a state it had just agreed not to rule.

counterparties.name: The Egba state at Abeokuta
counterparties.lost: Nothing on paper and a great deal in practice: an independence guaranteed by a neighbouring empire is an independence held on that empire's terms, and Britain revoked the guarantee twenty-one years later.

instrument.name: Anglo-Egba Treaty of 1893
instrument.note: Britain recognised Egbaland as an independent state. It is one of very few such recognitions given to an African polity inside a British sphere in the 1890s.

people.name: Gilbert Carter
people.role: Governor of Lagos, who signed the treaty and spent the 1890s bringing the other Yoruba states under British protection

people.name: Oyekan I
people.role: Alake of Abeokuta at the time of the treaty

evidence.author: Saburi O. Biobaku
evidence.work: The Egba and Their Neighbours 1842-1872
evidence.supports: The rise of Abeokuta and its dealings with Lagos and the missions.

acquisitions.how: Weeks after troops shot dead a large number of Ijemo people in Abeokuta in a dispute over a chief, Britain abolished the Egba United Government and absorbed Egbaland into the Protectorate of Southern Nigeria.

counterparties.name: The Egba United Government
counterparties.lost: An African-run state with its own treasury, courts, police, printing press and postal service — staffed by Yoruba men educated in Freetown and Lagos — was abolished by administrative order in a country Britain had recognised as independent.

people.name: Adegboyega Edun
people.role: secretary of the Egba United Government and the effective head of its administration until 1914

people.name: Gbadebo I
people.role: Alake of Abeokuta; visited Britain in 1904 and met Edward VII as the ruler of an independent state

people.name: Frederick Lugard
people.role: Governor-General of the newly amalgamated Nigeria, who ended Egba independence in his first year

acquisitions.resistance: The Adubi War of June 1918: Egba farmers rose against taxation and forced labour on the railway, cut the telegraph and blocked the roads. Troops with machine guns put it down and several hundred Egba were killed.

cost.note: For the Adubi rising of 1918. The figures come from British reports and a later commission; nobody counted independently, and the Ijemo killings of August 1914 have no agreed total at all.

warrant.author: The British administration, and the commission of inquiry into the Adubi rising
warrant.work: British reports and the inquiry into the Adubi rising
warrant.supports: For the Adubi rising of 1918. The figures come from British reports and a later commission; nobody counted independently, and the Ijemo killings of August 1914 have no agreed total at all.
warrant.check: Reports of colonial commissions and boards of inquiry are Command Papers: British Parliamentary Papers, and the CO series at The National Archives, Kew.
warrant.note: The Ijemo killings of 1914 had no inquiry and have no agreed total, which is the same fact seen from the other side.

contested.note: The exact date of the annexation and the death toll at Ijemo in August 1914 are both recorded loosely; the sequence — massacre, then annexation within weeks — is not in dispute.

statusPeriods.label: An independent African state inside a British sphere
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The Egba governed themselves: their own secretary, treasury, customs, police and courts, run largely by Saro returnees, while Britain guaranteed their independence and controlled the roads and railway through their territory.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Abeokuta, by the Alake and the Egba United Government
statusPeriods.franchise: The Egba government rested on the Ogboni council and the townships' own chiefs, not on a colonial franchise. It was self-government of a kind no British African colony had.
statusPeriods.note: In 1904 the Alake Gbadebo I travelled to England and was received by Edward VII as a fellow sovereign. Ten years later his state was abolished by a governor's order.

statusPeriods.label: Absorbed into Nigeria
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Abeokuta became a Native Authority under a Resident: the Alake kept his title and lost his government, and taxation, courts and the railway passed to British officials.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Abeokuta, under the Southern Provinces of Nigeria
statusPeriods.franchise: No elections. Taxation without representation was the direct grievance behind the 1918 rising and behind the women's revolt of 1946-49.
statusPeriods.note: In 1946 Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti's Abeokuta Women's Union — tens of thousands of market women — began a campaign against the tax on women that ended in January 1949 with the Alake, Ademola II, abdicating. He was allowed back in 1950. An African women's movement removed a British-backed ruler.

departures.how: Egbaland entered independent Nigeria as part of the Western Region, sixty-seven years after Britain had recognised it as a state and forty-six after abolishing it.

led.name: Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti
led.role: founder of the Abeokuta Women's Union and the Nigerian Women's Union; forced an Alake to abdicate and demanded the vote for women

led.name: Obafemi Awolowo
led.role: Premier of the Western Region, which Egbaland was part of

departures.movement: Action Group; the Abeokuta Women's Union

cost.note: Nobody died in 1960. Egba deaths belong to 1914 at Ijemo and to the Adubi rising of 1918.

departures.borders: Egbaland's boundaries became internal Nigerian ones and, from 1976, the borders of Ogun State.

violence.note: Two episodes: troops killed a disputed number of Ijemo people at Abeokuta in August 1914, and the Adubi rising of 1918 against tax and forced labour cost several hundred Egba lives.

toll.note: For the 1918 rising, from British reports. The 1914 Ijemo killings were never given an agreed total.

warrant.author: The British administration, and the commission of inquiry into the Adubi rising
warrant.work: British reports and the inquiry into the Adubi rising
warrant.supports: For the 1918 rising, from British reports. The 1914 Ijemo killings were never given an agreed total.
warrant.check: Reports of colonial commissions and boards of inquiry are Command Papers: British Parliamentary Papers, and the CO series at The National Archives, Kew.
warrant.note: The side doing the killing counted its own dead precisely and the other side’s by estimate. That asymmetry is in the figure, not just in the footnote.

populationTransfer.note: Abeokuta was built by refugees from the Yoruba wars and then repopulated by Saro — Yoruba people freed from slave ships at Freetown who came home literate, Christian and used to running institutions.

consequences.economicLegacy: The railway from Lagos to the north ran through Egbaland, and controlling it was the reason Britain could not tolerate an independent state on the line.
consequences.languageAndLaw: The Alake and the Ogboni survive as traditional institutions; the Egba experiment is remembered in Nigeria as evidence that Africans were running modern administrations before colonial rule reached them.

peak.populationNote: Estimates for Abeokuta and its farms around 1900 range from 60,000 to over 100,000; there was no census.

evidence.author: Saburi O. Biobaku
evidence.work: The Egba and Their Neighbours 1842-1872
evidence.supports: The founding of Abeokuta and its relations with Lagos, the missions and its neighbours.

evidence.author: Toyin Falola and Matthew M. Heaton
evidence.work: A History of Nigeria
evidence.supports: The Egba United Government, its abolition and the Abeokuta women's revolt.

evidence.author: J.F.A. Ajayi
evidence.work: Christian Missions in Nigeria 1841-1891: The Making of a New Elite
evidence.supports: The Saro returnees and the educated class that ran the Egba administration.

contested.note: The Egba case is used by each side of a bigger argument: as proof that Africans were building modern states before conquest, and as evidence that such states could not survive economically between a colonial port and a colonial railway. The dates of the 1914 annexation are also recorded loosely.

pedagogy.hook: In 1904 the ruler of Abeokuta was received by Edward VII as a fellow sovereign. Ten years later a British governor abolished his state with a memorandum.

misconception.belief: Africans had no experience of modern government before colonial rule taught them.
misconception.correction: The Egba United Government ran a treasury, a customs service, a police force, a postal service, courts and a printing press from Abeokuta, staffed by Yoruba men and women educated in Freetown and Lagos, and Britain formally recognised it as independent in 1893. It was abolished in 1914 not because it failed but because it stood on the railway line to the north.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Egbaland is the cleanest counter-example to the idea that colonial rule filled a vacuum. It also produced Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti, whose women's union forced a British-backed ruler off his throne in 1949 — one of the few times in colonial Africa that a mass movement of women won outright.

territories.name: British Cameroons
territories.formalName: The Trust Territory of the Cameroons under United Kingdom administration

namesOverTime.name: Kamerun
namesOverTime.note: From the Portuguese Rio dos Camarões, 'river of prawns', for the Wouri estuary.

namesOverTime.name: The British Cameroons
namesOverTime.note: Two separate strips, 500 km apart at their furthest points, administered as parts of two different Nigerian regions.

namesOverTime.name: The North-West and South-West regions of Cameroon, and parts of Adamawa, Taraba and Borno states in Nigeria
namesOverTime.note: The two halves of the mandate went to two different countries in 1961, four months apart, on the results of two plebiscites.

modernSuccessors.name: Nigeria
modernSuccessors.note: Northern Cameroons voted to join Nigeria and is now part of Borno, Adamawa and Taraba states.

modernSuccessors.name: Cameroon
modernSuccessors.note: Southern Cameroons joined the Republic of Cameroon as a federated state; the federation was abolished in 1972 and the region has been in armed conflict with the government since 2017.

geoCoverage.label: German Kamerun under Allied occupation
geoCoverage.change: British, French and Belgian forces took Duala on 27 September 1914 and spent seventeen months clearing the interior; the last German post at Mora surrendered in February 1916.

geoCoverage.label: Two strips along the Nigerian border
geoCoverage.change: Britain and France divided the conquered colony: France took four fifths including the capital, Britain took two narrow strips totalling about 88,000 square kilometres along the Nigerian frontier.

acquisitions.how: British and French troops, most of them West Africans, took the German port of Duala in September 1914 and spent the next seventeen months forcing the German garrison out of the interior.

counterparties.name: The German Empire
counterparties.lost: Germany lost Kamerun, a colony it had held for thirty years, and with it the plantations at the foot of Mount Cameroon built with forced labour.

counterparties.name: The peoples of Kamerun
counterparties.lost: They exchanged one European ruler for two. Tens of thousands were conscripted as carriers by the British and the French alike and an unknown number died on the marches.

cost.note: The Kamerun campaign killed a few thousand soldiers and a far larger, uncounted number of African carriers, who moved every shell and sack of rice through forest with no roads.

acquisitions.how: The League of Nations confirmed Britain's mandate over two strips of former Kamerun, on the argument that Germany was unfit to govern colonies and the victors were.

counterparties.name: The German Empire
counterparties.lost: Germany was stripped of every colony at Versailles and the territories were distributed to Britain, France, Belgium, South Africa, Japan, Australia and New Zealand as mandates.

counterparties.name: The peoples of the British Cameroons
counterparties.lost: They were placed under an administration whose declared purpose was to prepare them for self-rule, and which then governed them as an appendix of Nigeria for thirty-nine years.

instrument.name: League of Nations Mandate for the British Cameroons
instrument.note: The boundary with French Cameroun had been fixed by the Milner-Simon Declaration of 10 July 1919.

acquisitions.how: The United Nations turned the mandate into a trusteeship with visiting missions, a right of petition and an obligation to consult the inhabitants about their future.

counterparties.name: The peoples of the British Cameroons
counterparties.lost: Nothing was lost and something was gained: the right to petition the UN directly, which Cameroonian nationalists used relentlessly and which forced the plebiscites of 1959 and 1961.

instrument.name: Trusteeship Agreement for the Cameroons under United Kingdom administration

statusPeriods.label: Military occupation and Anglo-French partition
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British and French commanders divided the conquered colony between them in March 1916 by drawing the Picot line on a map; the line was adjusted in 1919 and became an international border.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Lagos and Buea

statusPeriods.label: League mandate administered as part of Nigeria
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain governed the two strips as though they were Nigerian provinces — the northern strip with the Northern Provinces, the southern with the Eastern — and reported annually to Geneva that it was preparing them for self-rule.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Lagos, with reports to the Permanent Mandates Commission in Geneva
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted. The territory had no institutions of its own at all.
statusPeriods.note: The German plantations on Mount Cameroon were sold at auction in London in 1924; German buyers bought most of them back, and were expropriated again in 1939.

statusPeriods.label: UN trust territory
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Administration continued through Nigeria, but UN visiting missions arrived, petitions flowed to New York, and from 1954 Southern Cameroons had its own House of Assembly at Buea inside the Nigerian federation.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Buea for the south and Kaduna for the north, under Lagos
statusPeriods.franchise: Southern Cameroonians elected their own assembly from 1954 and voted in the plebiscites of 1961; Northern Cameroonians voted in the plebiscites of 1959 and 1961.

departures.how: In the plebiscite of 11 February 1961 the northern strip voted by roughly 60 to 40 to join Nigeria, and it did so on 1 June 1961, eight months after Nigeria itself became independent.

led.name: Abubakar Tafawa Balewa
led.role: Prime Minister of Nigeria, whose government campaigned for the northern strip to join it

led.name: Ahmadou Ahidjo
led.role: President of Cameroon, who protested the result and took Britain to the International Court of Justice over it

departures.movement: Northern People's Congress and the northern emirates, against the Cameroon government

cost.note: The plebiscite was peaceful and nobody died. The cost was borne later by people who found themselves in the wrong country: Cameroon has never accepted the result.

departures.borders: The result put a strip of Adamawa and Borno into Nigeria and made the Picot line of 1916 permanent. Cameroon sued Britain at the International Court of Justice, which ruled on 2 December 1963 that it could not adjudicate because the trusteeship had already ended.

instrument.name: UN General Assembly Resolution 1608 (XV)
instrument.note: The resolution endorsed both plebiscite results and set the dates: 1 June 1961 for the north and 1 October 1961 for the south. Cameroon voted against it.

contested.note: Cameroon argued that the plebiscite was invalid because the north had been administered as part of Nigeria for forty years by officials who wanted that result, and because the ballot offered no option of independence. The ICJ declined to rule on the merits.

evidence.author: Victor Julius Ngoh
evidence.work: History of Cameroon Since 1800
evidence.supports: The plebiscites, the campaigns and the transfers of 1961.

departures.how: The southern strip voted by about 70 to 30 to join the Republic of Cameroon rather than Nigeria, and joined it as a federated state on 1 October 1961 on terms negotiated at Foumban three months earlier.

led.name: John Ngu Foncha
led.role: leader of the Kamerun National Democratic Party; campaigned for union with Cameroon and became Vice-President of the federation

led.name: Emmanuel Endeley
led.role: led the campaign to stay with Nigeria and lost the plebiscite

led.name: Ahmadou Ahidjo
led.role: President of Cameroon; negotiated the federal constitution at Foumban and dismantled it in 1972

cost.note: Nobody died in the 1961 transfer. The armed conflict that began in the same region in 2017 over the loss of its Anglophone institutions has killed several thousand people and displaced more than half a million.

departures.borders: The Picot line of 1916 became the Nigeria-Cameroon border. Britain never offered a third option of independence on either ballot, which is the grievance the Anglophone separatist movement still cites.

contested.note: Whether Southern Cameroons was given a real choice is disputed. The UN plebiscite offered union with Nigeria or union with Cameroon; independence was not on the ballot, although Southern Cameroons had its own legislature and premier. Separatists date their claim from this omission.

evidence.author: Piet Konings and Francis B. Nyamnjoh
evidence.work: Negotiating an Anglophone Identity: A Study of the Politics of Recognition and Representation in Cameroon
evidence.supports: The plebiscite, the Foumban constitution and the long Anglophone grievance.

partition.note: German Kamerun was partitioned in 1916 between Britain and France, and the British part was partitioned again in 1961, its two halves going to two different countries.
partition.lineDrawnBy: Charles Strachey and Georges Picot for Britain and France in March 1916, confirmed by the Milner-Simon Declaration of 1919

violence.note: The 1914-16 campaign killed thousands of soldiers and an uncounted number of conscripted African carriers; the Anglophone conflict that began in 2017 is the long consequence of the 1961 settlement.

consequences.borderLegacy: A line two European officials drew across Kamerun in March 1916 is now the Nigeria-Cameroon border and the fault line of a civil conflict.

commonwealth.note: Cameroon joined the Commonwealth in 1995 largely because of its Anglophone regions — the only French-ruled country to join on the strength of a British-administered minority.

consequences.languageAndLaw: The former British Cameroons still uses English and common law inside a country that is otherwise French-speaking and civil-law; the attempt to replace its courts and schools with the French system triggered the crisis of 2016-17.

peak.populationNote: The two strips together held roughly 1.6 million people at the 1953 census, but the figures were collected as part of Nigerian regional counts and are not cleanly separable. The Northern Cameroons shape in this atlas is an approximation drawn by the geometry team, and its mapped area is larger than the real one.

evidence.author: Piet Konings and Francis B. Nyamnjoh
evidence.work: Negotiating an Anglophone Identity: A Study of the Politics of Recognition and Representation in Cameroon
evidence.supports: The 1961 plebiscites, the federal bargain and the Anglophone question.

evidence.author: Victor Julius Ngoh
evidence.work: History of Cameroon Since 1800
evidence.supports: The German period, the Anglo-French partition and the trusteeship.

evidence.author: Toyin Falola and Matthew M. Heaton
evidence.work: A History of Nigeria
evidence.supports: The administration of the Cameroons as part of Nigeria and the 1961 transfers.

contested.note: The 1961 plebiscites are the most disputed decolonisation vote in West Africa. The argument is not about the count but about the question: no ballot offered independence, and the two halves of one territory were sent to two different countries on the same day's decision.

pedagogy.hook: British Cameroons is the only British territory that left the empire by voting itself into two different countries.

misconception.belief: Every colony became an independent country.
misconception.correction: Not all of them. British Cameroons was split in two by plebiscite in 1961: the northern strip joined Nigeria and the southern strip joined Cameroon, and neither ballot offered independence as an option. British Somaliland merged into Somalia, Italian-ruled territories were divided, and several small territories joined neighbours. Decolonisation produced mergers as well as new flags.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: This is the sharpest case of self-determination limited by the choices on offer. It also explains a war: the Anglophone conflict in Cameroon since 2017 is a direct descendant of a 1961 ballot with two options on it.

keyDates.what: Germany raises its flag over Kamerun, five days before the British consul arrives
Britain and France partition the conquered colony
League of Nations mandate confirmed
Plebiscites: the north votes for Nigeria, the south for Cameroon
Northern Cameroons joins Nigeria
Southern Cameroons joins Cameroon

territories.name: Southern Cameroons
territories.formalName: The Southern Cameroons
territories.subregion: Bamenda grassfields and the Mount Cameroon coast

namesOverTime.name: West Cameroon
namesOverTime.note: The federated state's name until the federation was abolished by referendum in 1972.

namesOverTime.name: Ambazonia
namesOverTime.note: The name used by separatists who declared the region's independence in 2017; it is not recognised by any state.

namesOverTime.name: The North-West and South-West Regions of Cameroon
namesOverTime.note: Cameroon's provinces became regions by decree in 2008. These two are the anglophone ones, and the separatist name Ambazonia is claimed over the same ground by people no state recognises.

modernSuccessors.name: Cameroon
modernSuccessors.note: Now Cameroon's North-West and South-West regions, in armed conflict with the central government since 2017.

geoCoverage.label: The southern strip: Buea, Victoria and the Bamenda grassfields
geoCoverage.change: About 42,000 square kilometres from the sea to the Benue watershed, administered from Buea as part of Nigeria's Eastern Region.

acquisitions.how: British and French officers drew a provisional line across the conquered German colony and Britain took the southern strip, which contained the plantations at the foot of Mount Cameroon and the grassfields kingdoms behind them.

counterparties.name: The German Empire
counterparties.lost: Germany lost the plantation economy it had built at Buea and Victoria with forced labour, and never got it back.

counterparties.name: The Bamileke, Bakweri, Bali, Nso and Kom peoples
counterparties.lost: The Bakweri had already lost most of their coastal land to German plantation companies. The new line put their neighbours and kin under French rule and them under British, without asking anyone.

acquisitions.how: The UN trusteeship gave Southern Cameroonians a right of petition, which they used so effectively that by 1954 they had their own House of Assembly at Buea and by 1958 their own Premier.

counterparties.name: The people of Southern Cameroons
counterparties.lost: Nothing at this step. The trusteeship is the reason they got a legislature and a plebiscite at all; Britain had run them as a Nigerian province for thirty years without one.

instrument.name: Trusteeship Agreement for the Cameroons under United Kingdom administration

statusPeriods.label: Occupied territory run from Nigeria
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: British officers governed the strip from Buea using German buildings and, for a while, German plantation records.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Buea, under Lagos

statusPeriods.label: Mandate administered as Nigerian provinces
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Southern Cameroons was divided into Nigerian provinces and administered from Enugu; its people were Nigerian for every practical purpose and Cameroonian in international law.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Buea and Enugu, under Lagos
statusPeriods.note: The German plantations were sold in London in 1924 and mostly bought back by German firms, which the Bakweri whose land it had been regarded as one theft compounding another.

statusPeriods.label: Trust territory with its own assembly
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: From 1954 Southern Cameroons had a House of Assembly at Buea, from 1958 a Premier, and from 1959 a quasi-federal status inside Nigeria — a self-governing territory that then voted to leave the country it was governed from.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Buea
statusPeriods.franchise: Universal adult suffrage in the elections of 1959 and in the plebiscite of 11 February 1961.

departures.how: 233,571 people voted to join the Republic of Cameroon and 97,741 to join Nigeria, and on 1 October 1961 Southern Cameroons became West Cameroon, a federated state with its own government, courts and schools.

led.name: John Ngu Foncha
led.role: Premier of Southern Cameroons and leader of the KNDP; won the plebiscite for union with Cameroon and negotiated the federal terms at Foumban

led.name: Emmanuel Endeley
led.role: former Premier who campaigned for union with Nigeria and lost

led.name: Ahmadou Ahidjo
led.role: President of Cameroon; abolished the federation in 1972

cost.note: Nobody died in 1961. The federal guarantees Foncha negotiated were dismantled by 1972, and armed conflict over that loss since 2017 has killed several thousand people and displaced over half a million.

departures.borders: The 1916 Picot line, drawn by two officers to divide a war prize, became Cameroon's western border and the boundary of its Anglophone regions.

contested.note: Whether this was self-determination is argued: the territory had a Premier, an assembly and a treasury, and the ballot offered it no option of keeping them as an independent state.

evidence.author: Piet Konings and Francis B. Nyamnjoh
evidence.work: Negotiating an Anglophone Identity: A Study of the Politics of Recognition and Representation in Cameroon
evidence.supports: The plebiscite figures, the Foumban conference and the erosion of the federal bargain.

violence.note: German plantation companies took most of the Bakweri coastal land by force before 1914; Britain sold it back to them in 1924; the Bakweri Land Claims Committee is still pursuing the case.

populationTransfer.note: The Mount Cameroon plantations pulled labour migrants from the grassfields and from Nigeria for eighty years, creating a coastal population with roots everywhere else.

consequences.borderLegacy: Southern Cameroons kept English, common law and its own school system inside a French-speaking, civil-law state, and the attempt to merge them caused the crisis of 2016-17.
consequences.languageAndLaw: English-language courts and Cambridge-style examinations survive in the North-West and South-West regions; lawyers and teachers defending them started the protests that became a war.

peak.populationNote: Around 850,000 people at the time of the 1961 plebiscite; 331,312 valid votes were cast in it. Colonial census figures for the territory were collected within Nigerian regional counts.

evidence.author: Piet Konings and Francis B. Nyamnjoh
evidence.work: Negotiating an Anglophone Identity: A Study of the Politics of Recognition and Representation in Cameroon
evidence.supports: The plebiscite, the federation and the Anglophone question.

evidence.author: Victor Julius Ngoh
evidence.work: History of Cameroon Since 1800
evidence.supports: The German plantations, the mandate and the 1961 settlement.

pedagogy.hook: Southern Cameroons had its own Premier, parliament and treasury in 1961, and the ballot it was given did not include the option of keeping them.

misconception.belief: A UN-supervised plebiscite means the people chose freely.
misconception.correction: Supervision guarantees the count, not the question. Southern Cameroonians were offered union with Nigeria or union with Cameroon. Independence, which a self-governing territory with its own premier might reasonably have expected, was ruled out in advance because the UN and Britain both thought it too small to stand alone. That single omission is the origin of a war still being fought.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest live consequence of a colonial decision anywhere in this atlas: a boundary drawn in 1916 and a ballot printed in 1961 are the direct cause of a conflict that has displaced over half a million people since 2017.

territories.name: Northern Cameroons
territories.formalName: The Northern Cameroons

namesOverTime.name: Northern Cameroons
namesOverTime.note: Two separate blocks — around Dikwa in the north and Adamawa in the south — administered as part of Nigeria's Northern Region.

namesOverTime.name: Parts of Adamawa, Taraba and Borno states, Nigeria

modernSuccessors.name: Nigeria
modernSuccessors.note: Now parts of Borno, Adamawa and Taraba states. Cameroon has never accepted the transfer.

geoCoverage.label: Two strips along the Nigerian border
geoCoverage.change: The geometry team could not reconstruct the exact 1916 line, so this shape is an approximation drawn along the Borno, Adamawa and Taraba frontier and is larger than the real 45,000 square kilometres.

acquisitions.how: Britain took the northern strip of German Kamerun in the Anglo-French partition, chiefly because the emirates in it were the eastern halves of emirates whose western halves were already British.

counterparties.name: The German Empire
counterparties.lost: Germany lost the northern half of Kamerun, including Dikwa and the Adamawa uplands.

counterparties.name: The emirates of Dikwa and Adamawa
counterparties.lost: They had already been cut in half by the Anglo-German boundary of 1893. In 1916 Britain reunited the pieces under one administration, and in 1961 the ballot separated some of them again.

contested.note: The 1916 Picot line was provisional and was adjusted by the Milner-Simon Declaration of 1919 and again in the 1930s; the boundary this atlas draws is an approximation.

acquisitions.how: The territory became a UN trust territory, which is why its people got two plebiscites — in 1959 and 1961 — while the Nigerian provinces beside them got none.

counterparties.name: The people of Northern Cameroons
counterparties.lost: Nothing at this step. The trusteeship gave them a vote on their own future that no other northern Nigerians had.

instrument.name: Trusteeship Agreement for the Cameroons under United Kingdom administration

statusPeriods.label: Occupied and attached to Northern Nigeria
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: The strip was administered from Kaduna as though it were part of Northern Nigeria, through the same emirs whose territory it had been before 1893.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kaduna, under Lagos

statusPeriods.label: Mandate governed as Nigerian emirates
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Indirect rule through the emirs of Dikwa and Adamawa, indistinguishable in daily practice from the Nigerian provinces on the other side of the line.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kaduna, with reports to Geneva
statusPeriods.franchise: Nobody voted.

statusPeriods.label: UN trust territory inside the Northern Region
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Nothing changed on the ground: the emirs ruled and Kaduna supervised. What changed was that the UN required a vote, and after the 1959 plebiscite chose to defer the decision, a second one was held in 1961.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Kaduna
statusPeriods.franchise: Adult male suffrage in the plebiscites of 7 November 1959 and 11 February 1961. Women in the Northern Region did not have the vote.

departures.how: 146,296 people voted to join Nigeria and 97,659 to join Cameroon, and on 1 June 1961 the strip became Nigerian, eight months after Nigeria itself became independent. Southern Cameroons did the same thing four months later, joining a Cameroon that had been independent since 1960.

led.name: Ahmadu Bello
led.role: Sardauna of Sokoto and Premier of the Northern Region, whose party organised the campaign for union with Nigeria

led.name: Ahmadou Ahidjo
led.role: President of Cameroon; rejected the result and sued Britain at the International Court of Justice

led.name: Abdoulaye Sanda
led.role: leader of the campaign in the territory for union with Cameroon, which lost by roughly 60 to 40

cost.note: Nobody died. The dispute went to the International Court of Justice instead, which on 2 December 1963 declined to rule because the trusteeship had already ended.

departures.borders: The vote made the 1916 line permanent and cut the emirates of Dikwa and Adamawa across an international border for the second time in seventy years.

instrument.name: UN General Assembly Resolution 1608 (XV)
instrument.note: Cameroon voted against the resolution and immediately took Britain to the International Court of Justice.

contested.note: Cameroon argued the plebiscite was rigged by forty years of administration from Kaduna and by a ballot that excluded independence. The ICJ dismissed the case on procedural grounds in 1963 without deciding whether Cameroon was right.

evidence.author: Victor Julius Ngoh
evidence.work: History of Cameroon Since 1800
evidence.supports: The 1959 and 1961 plebiscites in Northern Cameroons and the Cameroonian case against them.

partition.note: This strip was cut from Adamawa and Borno by the Anglo-German boundary of 1893, reattached to Nigeria by the Anglo-French partition of 1916, and confirmed Nigerian by plebiscite in 1961.
partition.lineDrawnBy: British and French officers in 1916, following an Anglo-German line of 1893

consequences.borderLegacy: The Nigeria-Cameroon border here separates people of the same emirates, languages and markets, and the dispute over it reached the International Court of Justice twice, in 1963 and again over the Bakassi peninsula in 2002.
consequences.languageAndLaw: The territory was governed through emirs and sharia courts under Nigerian indirect rule, and joining Nigeria in 1961 changed almost nothing about how it was administered.

peak.populationNote: Roughly 750,000 people; the figures come from Nigerian regional counts rather than a separate census. The shape drawn in this atlas is approximate and covers more ground than the real territory did.

evidence.author: Victor Julius Ngoh
evidence.work: History of Cameroon Since 1800
evidence.supports: The plebiscites and the transfer to Nigeria.

evidence.author: Toyin Falola and Matthew M. Heaton
evidence.work: A History of Nigeria
evidence.supports: The administration of Northern Cameroons within the Northern Region.

contested.note: Cameroon has never accepted the 1961 result and took Britain to the International Court of Justice over it. The Court's 1963 judgment did not decide the merits, so the grievance has no legal answer to this day.

pedagogy.hook: This strip of Africa left the British Empire by joining a country that had already been independent for eight months.

misconception.belief: Independence is what happens at the end of colonial rule.
misconception.correction: Not always. Northern Cameroons became part of Nigeria on 1 June 1961, eight months after Nigeria's own independence, because a plebiscite offered it two neighbours and no third choice. British Somaliland merged into Somalia the year before. Ending colonial rule and creating a state are two different events, and they do not always coincide.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the only case where a British territory's exit was tested in the International Court of Justice — and the Court refused to answer, which tells students something true about how international law handles decolonisation disputes.

territories.name: Ambas Bay and Victoria
territories.formalName: The British settlement and protectorate of Ambas Bay

namesOverTime.name: Victoria
namesOverTime.note: Founded by Alfred Saker and named after Queen Victoria.

namesOverTime.name: Limbe
namesOverTime.note: Renamed by the Cameroonian government.

modernSuccessors.name: Cameroon
modernSuccessors.note: German from 1887, British again from 1916, and Cameroonian since 1961.

geoCoverage.label: A mission town and its bay
geoCoverage.change: A few square kilometres at the foot of Mount Cameroon; no geo unit exists at this scale, so the map hatches Southern Cameroons and marks the town.

acquisitions.how: Alfred Saker, a Baptist missionary expelled from Spanish Fernando Po for being Protestant, bought land at Ambas Bay from King William of Bimbia and moved his congregation of freed Africans and Jamaicans there.

counterparties.name: The Isubu of Bimbia
counterparties.lost: King William sold a stretch of coast for trade goods and gained a mission town of strangers on it; within thirty years the whole coast belonged to a European empire.

instrument.name: Purchase of land at Ambas Bay from King William of Bimbia
instrument.note: Recorded in the Baptist Missionary Society's papers; the terms are given differently in different accounts.

people.name: Alfred Saker
people.role: Baptist missionary, printer and shipwright who founded Victoria and translated the Bible into Duala

people.name: King William of Bimbia
people.role: Isubu ruler who sold the land

evidence.author: Victor Julius Ngoh
evidence.work: History of Cameroon Since 1800
evidence.supports: The Baptist mission at Victoria and the British and German claims to the Cameroons coast.

acquisitions.how: Germany annexed Kamerun on 14 July 1884, five days before the British consul arrived to sign the treaty the Duala kings had been offering Britain for years; Britain claimed Victoria and Ambas Bay as the one piece it could still hold.

counterparties.name: The German Empire
counterparties.lost: Nothing, in the end: Germany got the rest of Kamerun and then Victoria too, three years later.

counterparties.name: The Duala kings Bell and Akwa
counterparties.lost: They had petitioned Britain repeatedly since the 1870s to annex their territory on terms they helped write. Britain dithered, Germany moved, and they got a treaty they had not chosen.

people.name: Edward Hyde Hewett
people.role: British consul who reached the Cameroons estuary on 19 July 1884, five days after the German flag went up; contemporaries called him 'Too-Late Hewett'

people.name: Gustav Nachtigal
people.role: German commissioner who signed the treaty with the Duala kings on 12 July 1884

contested.note: The status of Victoria between 1884 and 1887 is untidy in the records: Britain treated it as a protected settlement, Germany disputed the claim, and the two governments argued about it until Britain gave way.

statusPeriods.label: A mission settlement under no flag
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Saker's settlers governed themselves under a written constitution the mission drew up; Britain claimed nothing, and the Royal Navy called in when asked.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: the Baptist mission at Victoria
statusPeriods.franchise: The settlers elected their own council under the mission's constitution — a self-governing town of freed Africans and West Indians on a coast no European state claimed.

statusPeriods.label: A British claim Germany would not accept
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain declared the bay protected and put a consul there, while Germany insisted the whole coast was German and the Foreign Office worked out what to trade it for.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: the consulate at Victoria, under the Foreign Office

departures.how: Britain handed Victoria and Ambas Bay to Germany rather than quarrel over a mission town, and the Baptist mission sold its property to the Basel Mission and left.

led.name: Otto von Bismarck
led.role: German Chancellor, who had claimed the Cameroons coast in 1884 and pressed for the rest

led.name: Alfred Saker
led.role: founder of the settlement; he had died in 1880 and his community was handed over without being consulted

cost.note: Nobody died in the transfer. The settlers, most of them formerly enslaved people or their children, were not asked and had no say.

departures.borders: The transfer completed Germany's Kamerun. Britain got it all back as a conqueror in 1916, and the same coast is Cameroonian today.

instrument.name: Anglo-German agreement transferring Victoria and Ambas Bay to Germany
instrument.note: The exact date is given variously as March or later in 1887 in different accounts.

contested.note: Sources differ on the precise date and instrument of the cession; that Britain gave up Victoria to Germany in 1887 is not in doubt.

populationTransfer.note: Victoria was settled by freed Africans, Jamaicans and Cameroonians who had followed the Baptist mission from Fernando Po after Spain expelled Protestants in 1858.

consequences.borderLegacy: Britain's five-day delay in 1884 cost it the whole of Cameroon; the Duala kings had asked to be annexed by Britain for a decade and got Germany instead.
consequences.languageAndLaw: The Baptist mission's English-language schooling in Victoria is one root of the Anglophone identity that survives in south-west Cameroon today.

evidence.author: Victor Julius Ngoh
evidence.work: History of Cameroon Since 1800
evidence.supports: The Baptist settlement at Victoria, the German annexation of 1884 and the 1887 cession.

evidence.author: Thomas Pakenham
evidence.work: The Scramble for Africa 1876-1912
evidence.supports: The race for the Cameroons coast in July 1884 and Hewett's late arrival.

contested.note: The dates and legal form of Britain's claim to Ambas Bay between 1884 and 1887 are recorded inconsistently, which is why this record is marked medium confidence throughout.

pedagogy.hook: Britain lost Cameroon by five days: its consul reached the coast on 19 July 1884, and the German flag had gone up on the 14th.

misconception.belief: European powers seized African territory against the wishes of the Africans there, always and everywhere.
misconception.correction: The Duala kings Bell and Akwa spent a decade petitioning Britain to annex their territory, on conditions they wrote themselves about trade, courts and their own authority. They wanted a protector against their neighbours and against the traders' cheating. Britain hesitated, Germany moved first, and they got a worse bargain with another empire.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Scramble was a race with real contingency in it. A slow consul in 1884 is why Cameroon is a French-speaking country with an English-speaking minority, and why there is a war there now.

territories.name: Fernando Pó
territories.formalName: The British establishment at Port Clarence, Fernando Pó
territories.subregion: Island in the Bight of Biafra

from.note: The year the Portuguese navigator Fernão do Pó is said to have sighted the island; the date is uncertain.

namesOverTime.name: Port Clarence
namesOverTime.note: Named after the Duke of Clarence, later William IV; the Spanish renamed it Santa Isabel and it is now Malabo, the capital of Equatorial Guinea.

namesOverTime.name: Bioko
namesOverTime.note: The island's name since 1979; the Bubi people who live there have their own names for it.

modernSuccessors.name: Equatorial Guinea
modernSuccessors.note: Independent from Spain, not from Britain. Malabo, the capital, is the town the Royal Navy founded in 1827.

geoCoverage.label: The island only, not the mainland
geoCoverage.change: Britain occupied the island of Bioko with Spanish acquiescence; the geo unit also covers Río Muni on the mainland, which Britain never touched, so the shape is drawn hatched.

acquisitions.how: Captain William Fitzwilliam Owen founded a naval base and a town at Port Clarence, with Spanish acquiescence and no British title, to give the anti-slave-trade squadron a station 2,000 kilometres closer to the trade than Freetown was.

counterparties.name: The Kingdom of Spain
counterparties.lost: Spain had held the island in law since 1778 and had never occupied it. It let Britain use it and refused to sell it, and took it back when Britain lost interest.

counterparties.name: The Bubi people of the island
counterparties.lost: The Bubi had lived on the island for centuries and kept their distance from the coast. They were not consulted by Spain, by Britain, or by anyone who came later; their population fell steeply under Spanish plantation rule.

people.name: William Fitzwilliam Owen
people.role: naval captain and surveyor who founded Port Clarence and was its first superintendent

people.name: John Beecroft
people.role: British trader who became superintendent of the island and then, in 1843, the Spanish governor of it while also serving as British consul

contested.note: Britain's legal position on Fernando Pó was never settled: it occupied and administered the island for sixteen years without owning it, and negotiations to buy it from Spain in 1839-41 collapsed.

evidence.author: Padraic X. Scanlan
evidence.work: Freedom's Debtors: British Antislavery in Sierra Leone in the Age of Revolution
evidence.supports: The anti-slavery squadron, the Mixed Commission courts and the reasons Britain wanted a base further east.

statusPeriods.label: Naval base and Mixed Commission court
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: A British superintendent ran the town, the squadron used the harbour, and the courts that condemned captured slave ships sat there until the government moved them back to Freetown.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port Clarence, under the Admiralty and the Colonial Office
statusPeriods.note: The settlers were mostly Africans freed from captured slave ships, plus Krio from Freetown. Their descendants are the Fernandinos, still a distinct community in Malabo.

statusPeriods.label: Abandoned by the government, held by a trader
statusPeriods.howControlWorked: Britain withdrew its official establishment in 1834, and John Beecroft, a British trader, went on running the town on his own account with no legal authority from anyone.
statusPeriods.governedFrom: Port Clarence, by a private British trader
statusPeriods.note: Britain tried to buy the island outright from Spain in 1839-41 for a sum reported at £50,000 to £60,000. Spanish opinion and British parliamentary economy killed the deal.

departures.how: Spain sent an expedition to reassert its sovereignty, raised its flag over the town Britain had built, and appointed the resident British trader John Beecroft as its governor.

led.name: Juan José de Lerena
led.role: Spanish naval officer who raised the Spanish flag at Santa Isabel in 1843

led.name: John Beecroft
led.role: British trader appointed Spanish governor of the island and simultaneously British consul for the Bights from 1849

cost.note: Nobody died. The handover was a flag-raising and a change of letterhead.

departures.borders: Britain gave up the island and kept the consulate on it, which is why the man who directed the bombardment of Lagos in 1851 was operating from Spanish territory.

contested.note: Because Britain never held legal title, historians describe the end of the British presence variously as a withdrawal in 1834, a lapse, or a Spanish reassertion in 1843. This record dates it to 1843, when Spanish authority was actually exercised.

slavery.note: The island was Britain's forward base against the slave trade for seven years, and its Court of Mixed Commission condemned ships and freed the people aboard them.

toll.note: The number of people landed at Port Clarence from condemned ships is not separately recorded; most Liberated Africans were taken to Freetown, where between 90,000 and 100,000 were landed over the period.

populationTransfer.note: Freed Africans and Krio settlers brought from Sierra Leone founded the Fernandino community, which still exists in Malabo and speaks an English-based creole.

consequences.languageAndLaw: Pichinglis, an English-based creole descended from this settlement and from Krio, is still spoken on Bioko in an otherwise Spanish-speaking country.

evidence.author: Padraic X. Scanlan
evidence.work: Freedom's Debtors: British Antislavery in Sierra Leone in the Age of Revolution
evidence.supports: The anti-slavery squadron and its bases and courts.

evidence.author: Robert Smith
evidence.work: The Lagos Consulate 1851-1861
evidence.supports: John Beecroft's double role as Spanish governor and British consul.

contested.note: Britain's tenure here is genuinely ambiguous: an occupation without title, a withdrawal without a treaty, and a British consul who governed a Spanish island. Different accounts date the end of the British presence to 1834, 1843 or 1855.

pedagogy.hook: For eleven years the governor of this Spanish island was a British trader who was also Britain's consul, and he used it as a base to bombard Lagos.

misconception.belief: The map of empires was clear: each territory belonged to one power and everyone knew which.
misconception.correction: Fernando Pó was Spanish in law, British in practice, run by a British trader appointed by Spain, and used by the Royal Navy as a court and a coaling station. The empire's edges were full of arrangements like this. A map with clean colours is a simplification of something much messier.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: This island is where Britain's anti-slavery navy and its informal empire in the Bights of Benin and Biafra met. The consulate here is the direct ancestor of the Oil Rivers Protectorate and therefore of Nigeria.
