events.title: The Royal African Company chartered

endDate.note: The company's forts were transferred to the African Company of Merchants in 1752; the corporation was wound up over the following years.

events.summary: Charles II granted a monopoly of English trade with West Africa to a company whose governor was his brother James, Duke of York. Its business was gold, ivory and, above all, people.
events.significance: The Royal African Company shipped more enslaved Africans than any other single institution in the history of the Atlantic trade, and it built the forts — Cape Coast, Anomabu, James Island, Bunce — that became the skeleton of British West Africa 200 years later.

places.name: Cape Coast Castle
places.note: The company's African headquarters.

people.name: James, Duke of York
people.role: governor of the company; later King James II. Captives were branded with his initials

people.name: John Locke
people.role: philosopher of liberty and shareholder in the company

people.name: Philip Quaque
people.role: Fante boy sent to England and ordained in 1765 as the first African priest of the Church of England; chaplain at Cape Coast Castle for fifty years

toll.note: People embarked on Royal African Company ships between 1672 and 1731. The lower figure counts survivors of the crossing and the higher counts those forced aboard; both come from the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database and from William Pettigrew's work on the company's own records.

pedagogy.hook: The Royal African Company branded the people it shipped with the initials of its governor, the future King James II.

misconception.belief: The British slave trade was run by rogue traders outside the law.
misconception.correction: For its first quarter-century it was a legal monopoly held by a royal corporation whose governor was the king's brother and whose shareholders included John Locke, Samuel Pepys and much of the London merchant elite. Parliament opened the trade to everyone in 1698 because private traders complained the monopoly was unfair, and the volume then rose sharply.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It shows the state at the centre of the trade, not on its edge — and it explains why so many places in this atlas begin as a fort belonging to a company rather than a colony belonging to a Crown.

evidence.author: William A. Pettigrew
evidence.work: Freedom's Debt: The Royal African Company and the Politics of the Atlantic Slave Trade, 1672-1752
evidence.supports: The company's charter, monopoly, politics and volume of trafficking.

evidence.author: William St Clair
evidence.work: The Grand Slave Emporium: Cape Coast Castle and the British Slave Trade
evidence.supports: The daily operation of the company's forts.

events.title: The Province of Senegambia
events.summary: Britain joined the captured French post at Saint-Louis to its Gambia forts and made them a single Crown colony with a governor and council: the first British Crown colony anywhere in Africa.
events.significance: It shows that Britain was governing African territory a century before the Scramble, and that it was willing to trade such territory away again: Senegal went back to France in 1783 in the same settlement that recognised American independence.

places.name: Saint-Louis
places.note: The provincial capital.

people.name: Charles O'Hara
people.role: first governor, 1766-1775; recalled after complaints that he traded on his own account

evidence.author: John D. Hargreaves
evidence.work: Prelude to the Partition of West Africa
evidence.supports: The creation, administration and dissolution of the province.

contested.note: The province is thinly documented and historians differ over whether it was a serious experiment in Crown government in Africa or a wartime improvisation nobody in London wanted to fund.

events.title: The Slave Trade Act 1807
events.summary: Parliament made it illegal for British subjects to carry enslaved people across the Atlantic. It freed nobody who was already enslaved, and it left slavery legal in the British colonies for another 26 years.
events.significance: It turned Britain from the largest carrier in the Atlantic into the trade's principal policeman, and it gave Freetown, Fernando Po and the West Africa Squadron a purpose that later became a reason to claim territory.

places.name: Freetown
places.note: Base of the West Africa Squadron and seat of the Courts of Mixed Commission.

people.name: William Wilberforce
people.role: led the parliamentary campaign for twenty years

people.name: Olaudah Equiano
people.role: formerly enslaved author whose 1789 narrative was the abolition movement's most effective document; died in 1797, ten years before the Act

people.name: Thomas Clarkson
people.role: collected the evidence, including the ships' measurements that produced the Brookes diagram

toll.note: People embarked on British ships across the whole trade to 1807, from the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database. Roughly 400,000 to 600,000 of them died before landing. These are reconstructions from surviving voyage records and are a documented floor.

pedagogy.hook: The Act that abolished the British slave trade freed exactly nobody: every enslaved person in the empire on 26 March 1807 was still enslaved on 27 March.

misconception.belief: Britain abolished slavery in 1807.
misconception.correction: 1807 abolished the trade — carrying people across the Atlantic. Slavery itself remained legal in British colonies until the Act of 1833, which took effect in 1834 and then imposed four more years of unpaid 'apprenticeship' until 1838. And in territories Britain conquered later, such as Northern Nigeria, slavery survived British rule until 1936.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Abolition was real and it was fought for from below, by enslaved people in the Caribbean and by African and Black British campaigners, as well as argued for in Parliament. Holding that together with the fact that Britain had built the biggest trafficking operation in the Atlantic is the whole skill this subject demands.

evidence.author: David Eltis and David Richardson
evidence.work: Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade
evidence.supports: Volumes carried by British ships and the geography of embarkation.

evidence.author: Adam Hochschild
evidence.work: Bury the Chains: The British Struggle to Abolish Slavery
evidence.supports: The abolition campaign, its methods and its people.

events.title: The Bond of 1844
events.summary: Eight Fante chiefs signed a short document at Cape Coast acknowledging British jurisdiction over murder and robbery in their territories. It was three sentences long and it became the legal foundation of the Gold Coast Colony.
events.significance: Britain built a colony on it: the Bond was cited for thirty years as proof that the coastal states had consented to British authority. Ghana chose 6 March 1957 as its independence day so that the anniversary of the Bond would become the anniversary of its end.

places.name: Cape Coast Castle
places.note: Where the Bond was signed.

people.name: Henry Worsley Hill
people.role: Lieutenant-Governor who obtained the chiefs' signatures

people.name: George Maclean
people.role: his predecessor, whose informal arbitration of Fante disputes in the 1830s created the jurisdiction the Bond wrote down

pedagogy.hook: Ghana picked its independence date so that the anniversary of the day Fante chiefs signed away their courts would become the anniversary of getting them back.

misconception.belief: Colonial rule began when a European army arrived.
misconception.correction: On the Gold Coast it began with a piece of paper about criminal jurisdiction. The Bond conceded only that British officers could try murder and robbery. Thirty years later Britain cited it as consent to a Crown colony over the whole coast. Small legal concessions were how a great deal of the empire started.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest example anywhere in this atlas of a document meaning one thing when signed and something much larger when enforced.

evidence.author: David Kimble
evidence.work: A Political History of Ghana: The Rise of Gold Coast Nationalism, 1850-1928
evidence.supports: The Bond, Maclean's jurisdiction and their later constitutional use.

events.title: The bombardment of Lagos
events.summary: Royal Navy ships shelled Lagos for three days, drove out Oba Kosoko and installed his rival Akitoye, who signed a treaty against the slave trade a week later. Much of the town burned.
events.significance: It is the moment Britain's anti-slavery policy turned into territorial power on the Nigerian coast. Ten years later Lagos was annexed, and everything that became Nigeria was administered outward from it.

people.name: Kosoko
people.role: Oba of Lagos, driven out by the bombardment

people.name: Akitoye
people.role: installed by the British in his place

people.name: John Beecroft
people.role: British consul who pressed for the attack

toll.note: British losses were a few dozen killed and wounded across two attempts. Lagos casualties were never counted and were far higher; much of the town was destroyed by shellfire.

pedagogy.hook: Britain burned Lagos to stop the slave trade, then kept the town and taxed the trade that replaced it.

misconception.belief: Anti-slavery and empire-building were opposites.
misconception.correction: On this coast they were the same operation. Suppressing the trade required consuls, treaties, warships and, in the end, territory — and the territory turned out to be commercially useful. Both motives are in the same despatches from the same officials in the same months.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the hinge between the anti-slavery era and the colonial one, and it happened in the city that is now the largest in Africa.

evidence.author: Robert Smith
evidence.work: The Lagos Consulate 1851-1861
evidence.supports: The attack, its justification and its consequences.

events.title: The Fante Confederation
events.summary: Fante kings, chiefs and educated professionals meeting at Mankessim wrote a constitution for a self-governing confederation with a legislature, a national fund, schools and roads. British officials arrested its leaders for treasonable conspiracy within weeks.
events.significance: It is the earliest written African constitution for a modern representative state on the Gold Coast, and Britain broke it three years before annexing the same coast — which makes the standard story of Britain teaching Africans self-government hard to sustain here.

places.name: Mankessim
places.note: Where the constitution was drafted.

people.name: James Africanus Beale Horton
people.role: Sierra Leonean doctor and army surgeon whose West African Countries and Peoples (1868) argued for African self-government and inspired the Confederation

people.name: John Aggery
people.role: King of Cape Coast, deposed and deported by the British in 1866 for asserting his own jurisdiction

people.name: Charles Salmon
people.role: acting British administrator who arrested the Confederation's leaders in December 1871

pedagogy.hook: Three years before Britain declared the Gold Coast a colony, Fante leaders wrote their own constitution for it, and Britain arrested them for treason.

misconception.belief: Africans learned representative government from British colonial rule.
misconception.correction: The Fante Confederation of 1871 had a written constitution, an elected assembly, a fund for roads and schools and a plan for a national judiciary — designed by African kings and by professionals trained in Freetown and Britain. The British administrator's response was to arrest them. Colonial rule interrupted this experiment; it did not begin it.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the single strongest piece of evidence for the argument that African political modernity predates colonial rule rather than descending from it.

evidence.author: David Kimble
evidence.work: A Political History of Ghana: The Rise of Gold Coast Nationalism, 1850-1928
evidence.supports: The Confederation's constitution, membership and suppression.

events.title: The Sagrenti War and the burning of Kumasi
events.summary: Asante invaded the coast after Britain took Elmina and refused to pay the rent Asante claimed on it. Garnet Wolseley's expedition marched to Kumasi, burned the city on 4 February 1874, and imposed an indemnity of 50,000 ounces of gold.
events.significance: The war made a Crown colony possible: five months after Kumasi burned, Britain proclaimed the Gold Coast Colony over the coastal states. Asante calls the war after 'Sagrenti', its rendering of 'Sir Garnet'.

places.name: Kumasi
places.note: Burned on 4 February 1874.

places.name: Amoaful
places.note: The main battle, 31 January 1874.

people.name: Garnet Wolseley
people.role: commanded the British expedition; the campaign made his reputation and the phrase 'all Sir Garnet'

people.name: Kofi Karikari
people.role: Asantehene, deposed by his own council after the defeat

people.name: Amankwatia IV
people.role: Asante general who commanded the 1873 invasion of the coast and was killed at Amoaful

toll.note: British and West Indian losses were a few dozen killed and many more sick; Asante losses at Amoaful and on the retreat were counted only in British estimates and ran into the thousands. No Asante count survives.

evidence.author: Ivor Wilks
evidence.work: Asante in the Nineteenth Century: The Structure and Evolution of a Political Order
evidence.supports: The causes of the war, the Elmina note and the Asante state's response to defeat.

evidence.author: Robert B. Edgerton
evidence.work: The Fall of the Asante Empire
evidence.supports: The military course of the Anglo-Asante wars.

events.title: The Berlin Conference
events.summary: Fourteen states met in Bismarck's Berlin to agree rules for claiming African territory: free navigation of the Niger and Congo, notification of new coastal annexations, and 'effective occupation'. No African state was represented.
events.significance: It did not carve up Africa, but it set the terms of the race — and it is why Britain proclaimed the Oil Rivers Protectorate four months later and chartered the Royal Niger Company the year after that.

places.name: Berlin
places.note: The conference met at the Reich Chancellery on Wilhelmstrasse.

people.name: Otto von Bismarck
people.role: called and chaired the conference

people.name: Leopold II of the Belgians
people.role: obtained recognition of his personal claim to the Congo, which he then ran as private property

pedagogy.hook: Fourteen countries met to agree rules for taking Africa, and not one African state was in the room.

misconception.belief: The Berlin Conference divided Africa between the European powers with lines on a map.
misconception.correction: It agreed procedures, not borders: free trade in the Congo basin, free navigation of the Niger and Congo, and a rule that a coastal claim had to be notified and backed by effective occupation. The borders were fixed afterwards by dozens of bilateral treaties and twenty years of fighting on the ground, against people who fought back — Asante, Sokoto, Benin, Bai Bureh's Temne.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It explains the pace of what followed. 'Effective occupation' meant that a claim on paper had to be turned into soldiers and administrators quickly, which is exactly what Britain did between 1885 and 1903 across West Africa.

evidence.author: Thomas Pakenham
evidence.work: The Scramble for Africa 1876-1912
evidence.supports: The conference, its participants and what it did and did not decide.

evidence.author: John Iliffe
evidence.work: Africans: The History of a Continent
evidence.supports: The African context of the partition and African responses to it.

events.title: The Royal Niger Company chartered
events.summary: The Crown gave George Goldie's company the right to govern, tax and police the Niger and Benue basins. It had a constabulary of a few hundred men and it claimed a territory larger than France.
events.significance: Chartered companies let Britain claim African territory without paying for it. When the bluff had to be made real, the Crown revoked the charter, paid the shareholders £865,000, and conquered the Sokoto Caliphate itself.

places.name: Asaba
places.note: The company's headquarters on the Niger.

places.name: Akassa
places.note: Company depot destroyed by the Nembe in January 1895.

people.name: George Taubman Goldie
people.role: founder; bought out his rivals, collected treaties and sold the result to the Crown

people.name: Koko Mingi VIII
people.role: King of Nembe, who led the attack on the company's depot at Akassa in January 1895 after its monopoly ruined his people's trade

pedagogy.hook: A London company with about 400 soldiers was given the legal right to govern an area larger than France.

misconception.belief: The British government conquered Nigeria.
misconception.correction: For fourteen years a shareholder company did the claiming. The Royal Niger Company collected treaties, levied customs, ran courts and fought wars on the Niger, and the government could disown it when things went wrong. Only in 1900 did the Crown buy it out for £865,000 and send its own troops. The same pattern runs through the East India Company and the British South Africa Company.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the cheapest trick in the imperial repertoire: sovereignty by subcontract. Understand it here and the East India Company, Rhodesia and British East Africa all make sense.

evidence.author: Toyin Falola and Matthew M. Heaton
evidence.work: A History of Nigeria
evidence.supports: The company's charter, operations and revocation.

evidence.author: John D. Hargreaves
evidence.work: Prelude to the Partition of West Africa
evidence.supports: The Anglo-French treaty race on the Niger.

events.title: The Benin punitive expedition
events.summary: After an unauthorised British party was ambushed on the road to Benin in January, about 1,200 men stormed the city, burned it, deposed the Oba and removed thousands of brass plaques, ivories and carvings, which were auctioned in London.
events.significance: It ended a kingdom six centuries old and produced the most disputed objects in the world's museums. The Benin Bronzes are now in roughly 160 institutions and the argument about returning them has reshaped how museums explain themselves.

places.name: Ugbine
places.note: Where the Phillips party was ambushed on 4 January 1897.

people.name: Ovonramwen Nogbaisi
people.role: Oba of Benin; deposed, tried and exiled to Calabar, where he died in 1914

people.name: Harry Rawson
people.role: rear-admiral commanding the expedition

people.name: James Phillips
people.role: acting Consul-General who marched on Benin during a sacred festival after being told not to, and was killed with most of his party

toll.note: Nine of the ten Britons in the January party were killed, along with most of their roughly 220 African carriers. Benin's dead in February were never counted. The city burned for days and a large part of it was destroyed.

pedagogy.hook: The expedition that destroyed Benin was paid for by auctioning the art it took from Benin.

misconception.belief: Museum objects from Africa were mostly collected, bought or given.
misconception.correction: Some were. The Benin Bronzes were not. They were taken from a royal palace by a military expedition that had just burned the city, and the Foreign Office explicitly sold part of the haul to defray the cost of the operation. The paper trail exists, which is why this case is argued on documents rather than on feelings.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the clearest test of what museums are for, and it is live: Germany transferred ownership of over a thousand Benin objects to Nigeria in 2022 and other institutions have followed.

evidence.author: Dan Hicks
evidence.work: The Brutish Museums: The Benin Bronzes, Colonial Violence and Cultural Restitution
evidence.supports: The expedition, the looting and the dispersal of the objects.

evidence.author: Robert Home
evidence.work: City of Blood Revisited: A New Look at the Benin Expedition of 1897
evidence.supports: The military narrative and the press campaign that justified it.

contested.note: Whether the January ambush was ordered by the Oba, by chiefs acting against his wishes, or was a predictable result of Phillips marching in during a festival he had been warned about, is still argued.

events.title: The Hut Tax War
events.summary: Sierra Leone's new Protectorate imposed a tax of five shillings a year on every house. Bai Bureh fought British columns in Temne country for ten months, and a separate rising in Mende country killed hundreds of Krio traders and missionaries.
events.significance: A British inquiry under Sir David Chalmers concluded that the tax caused the war and should be dropped. The governor disagreed, London backed the governor, and the tax stayed — which tells students how colonial inquiries usually ended.

places.name: Kasseh
places.note: Bai Bureh's town in Temne country.

people.name: Bai Bureh
people.role: ruler of Kasseh; fought British columns for ten months without losing a battle in the field, surrendered when his people were starving, and was exiled to the Gold Coast until 1905

people.name: Frederic Cardew
people.role: governor who imposed the tax and rejected the inquiry that blamed it

people.name: David Chalmers
people.role: royal commissioner whose 1899 report blamed the hut tax and was overruled

toll.note: No count was kept of African deaths. British columns burned hundreds of villages and about a hundred men were hanged after trial. Several hundred Krio traders, missionaries and their families were killed in the Mende rising. The range is a historians' reconstruction.

pedagogy.hook: Bai Bureh fought the British army for ten months in 1898 and was never beaten in battle; he surrendered because his people were starving.

misconception.belief: Africans resisted colonial rule with spears against machine guns and lost quickly.
misconception.correction: Bai Bureh fought a guerrilla campaign: stockades, ambushes, night attacks, and a refusal to give the British a battle they could win. It took a large force ten months to end it, and only by burning the villages that fed his fighters. Resistance was tactical, and the British commanders said so in their own reports.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It also shows the colonial inquiry as a genre: Chalmers found the tax was the cause, the governor disagreed, and the tax stayed. Reports rarely changed policy; they recorded it.

evidence.author: Christopher Fyfe
evidence.work: A History of Sierra Leone
evidence.supports: The war, its causes, its suppression and the Chalmers report.

contested.note: Death tolls are estimates: nobody counted African dead, and the two risings — Bai Bureh's in the north and the Mende rising in the south — are sometimes treated as one war and sometimes as two.

events.title: The War of the Golden Stool
events.summary: Governor Frederick Hodgson came to Kumasi, demanded the Golden Stool and asked why it had not been produced for him to sit on. Yaa Asantewaa, Queen Mother of Ejisu, rallied the chiefs and besieged the British fort for three months.
events.significance: It was the last Anglo-Asante war and the reason Britain annexed Asante outright in 1902. The Golden Stool was never handed over: it was hidden in the forest and only found by accident in 1920.

places.name: Kumasi
places.note: The British fort was besieged here from late April to mid-July 1900.

places.name: Ejisu
places.note: Yaa Asantewaa's town.

people.name: Yaa Asantewaa
people.role: Queen Mother of Ejisu; told the chiefs that if the men would not fight, the women would, and led the rising. Exiled to the Seychelles, where she died in 1921

people.name: Frederick Hodgson
people.role: governor whose demand for the Golden Stool caused the war

people.name: James Willcocks
people.role: commanded the relief force that broke the siege

toll.note: Roughly 1,000 dead on the British side, most of them African soldiers and carriers and many from disease, and around 2,000 Asante. The figures come from British military returns; no Asante count was taken.

pedagogy.hook: A British governor asked to sit on the Golden Stool. It is the soul of the Asante nation, no Asantehene has ever sat on it, and it is not allowed to touch the ground.

misconception.belief: Colonial wars were caused by economics and strategy; culture was decoration.
misconception.correction: Hodgson's demand was a demand for the Asante nation's soul, and everyone in the room except Hodgson knew it. The Golden Stool is not a throne: it holds the spirit of the people, it has never been sat on, and it is not permitted to touch the earth. Misreading it started a war that killed thousands and ended Asante independence.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The best-known leader of anti-colonial resistance in West Africa was a woman in her sixties, and she is remembered by name across Ghana today while the governor is not.

evidence.author: A. Adu Boahen
evidence.work: Yaa Asantewaa and the Asante-British War of 1900-1
evidence.supports: The demand, the rising, its leadership and its suppression.

evidence.author: T.C. McCaskie
evidence.work: State and Society in Pre-colonial Asante
evidence.supports: The meaning of the Golden Stool in Asante political thought.

events.title: The conquest of the Sokoto Caliphate
events.summary: Lugard's force of about a thousand African soldiers with Maxim guns took Kano in February and Sokoto in March 1903. The Caliph Attahiru I refused to submit, led thousands east on a religious migration, and was killed at Burmi in July.
events.significance: It ended the largest independent state in nineteenth-century Africa and created the model of indirect rule that Britain then exported across its African empire: keep the rulers, take the sovereignty, govern on the cheap.

places.name: Kano
places.note: Walls breached by artillery on 3 February 1903.

places.name: Sokoto
places.note: Taken 15 March 1903.

places.name: Burmi
places.note: Where Attahiru I was killed on 27 July 1903.

people.name: Muhammadu Attahiru I
people.role: Caliph; refused submission, led a hijra east and was killed at Burmi with hundreds of his followers

people.name: Frederick Lugard
people.role: High Commissioner; conquered the caliphate and then ruled through the men he had defeated

people.name: Muhammadu Attahiru II
people.role: installed as Sultan by Lugard within days of the conquest

toll.note: British losses were counted in dozens and were mostly African soldiers. Caliphate deaths at Kano, Sokoto and Burmi were never counted; the range comes from British officers' estimates and is wide.

pedagogy.hook: The largest state in Africa in 1900 fell in eight weeks, and its conqueror reappointed its rulers within days of defeating them.

misconception.belief: Britain replaced African rulers with British administrators.
misconception.correction: In Northern Nigeria it did the opposite. Lugard kept the emirs, their courts, their sharia law and their tax machinery, and made them answerable to a British Resident who could depose them. About 350 British officials governed over ten million people because they were running somebody else's state, not building one.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Indirect rule was invented here and copied everywhere. It made the empire astonishingly cheap and made it collapse fast when the cooperation it depended on was withdrawn.

evidence.author: Murray Last
evidence.work: The Sokoto Caliphate
evidence.supports: The caliphate's structure and its fall.

evidence.author: Frederick Lugard
evidence.work: The Dual Mandate in British Tropical Africa
evidence.supports: The doctrine of indirect rule as its author stated it.

events.title: The amalgamation of Nigeria
events.summary: Frederick Lugard joined the Protectorates of Northern and Southern Nigeria and the Colony of Lagos into one Colony and Protectorate of Nigeria, chiefly so that southern customs revenue could pay for the northern administration.
events.significance: It created Africa's most populous country out of an accounting problem, and it kept the two halves legally, educationally and religiously separate inside the new border — a structure that produced the regional politics of the 1950s and the civil war of 1967.

places.name: Lagos
places.note: Seat of the new Governor-General.

people.name: Frederick Lugard
people.role: Governor-General who carried out the amalgamation and abolished the independent Egba state in the same year

people.name: Flora Shaw
people.role: journalist who coined the name Nigeria in 1897 and married Lugard in 1902

pedagogy.hook: Nigeria was created on 1 January 1914 so that palm-oil revenue from the south could pay the salaries of officials in the north.

misconception.belief: Colonial borders were drawn ignorantly, and that is why African states struggle.
misconception.correction: The border around Nigeria was drawn deliberately and for stated reasons: revenue. But the more consequential line was internal — Lugard kept North and South under separate laws, separate school systems and separate policies on Christian missions. Nigeria's difficulties come at least as much from what was done inside the border as from where the border was.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the founding act of the country that now holds one in every six Africans, and Nigerians still argue about it in exactly these terms.

evidence.author: Toyin Falola and Matthew M. Heaton
evidence.work: A History of Nigeria
evidence.supports: The amalgamation, its financial motive and its consequences.

evidence.author: Michael Crowder
evidence.work: The Story of Nigeria
evidence.supports: Lugard's administration and the structure it created.

contested.note: Nigerians argue about the amalgamation to this day: whether it made a viable country or forced together two systems Britain then took care to keep apart.

events.title: The Aba Women's War
events.summary: Tens of thousands of Igbo and Ibibio women mobilised across south-eastern Nigeria against the warrant chiefs and the fear of a tax on women, using the traditional sanction of 'sitting on a man'. Troops opened fire, killing at least fifty-one.
events.significance: It was the largest anti-colonial mobilisation in British West Africa before the Second World War, it was organised entirely by women, and it forced Britain to dismantle the warrant chief system it had imposed on Igbo society.

places.name: Oloko
places.note: Where the movement began after a census enumerator counted a woman's goats.

places.name: Opobo
places.note: Where troops fired on the crowd on 16 December 1929.

people.name: Nwanyeruwa
people.role: woman of Oloko whose argument with a census enumerator in November 1929 set the movement off

people.name: Ikonnia, Nwannedia and Nwugo
people.role: leaders of the Oloko women who carried the protest to the district officer

toll.note: Counted by the two British commissions of inquiry that followed. About fifty more women were wounded. No British or police deaths were recorded.

pedagogy.hook: In 1929 tens of thousands of Nigerian women brought colonial administration in the south-east to a halt, and British troops shot fifty-one of them dead.

misconception.belief: Anti-colonial politics was made by educated men in cities.
misconception.correction: The largest protest in British West Africa before 1939 was organised by market women in villages, through women's councils and age grades that predated colonial rule, using an established sanction called 'sitting on a man' — surrounding an offender, singing about his conduct until he made amends. Britain had abolished the political institutions women held and did not notice they still worked.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It forced a real policy change: the warrant chief system was investigated, reformed and largely dismantled. Very few colonial protests achieved that, and this one was made by people with no vote, no newspaper and no party.

evidence.author: Judith Van Allen
evidence.work: Sitting on a Man: Colonialism and the Lost Political Institutions of Igbo Women
evidence.supports: Igbo women's political institutions and how colonial rule erased them.

evidence.author: Adiele E. Afigbo
evidence.work: The Warrant Chiefs: Indirect Rule in Southeastern Nigeria 1891-1929
evidence.supports: The warrant chief system and the reforms that followed the rising.

events.title: The Accra riots
events.summary: Police fired on ex-servicemen marching to Christiansborg Castle to present a petition about their war pensions, killing three. Three days of rioting followed in Accra, Kumasi and Koforidua, and 29 people died.
events.significance: It turned Gold Coast politics from a lawyers' campaign into a mass movement. The Watson Commission that investigated it recommended a new constitution, and the six leaders Britain arrested became the men who took power.

places.name: Christiansborg crossroads, Osu, Accra
places.note: Where the shooting happened; a monument to Sergeant Adjetey stands there.

people.name: Cornelius Adjetey
people.role: sergeant and Second World War veteran shot dead on the road to the castle

people.name: Kwame Nkrumah
people.role: general secretary of the UGCC, arrested after the riots and released; founded the Convention People's Party the next year

people.name: J.B. Danquah
people.role: founder of the United Gold Coast Convention, arrested with Nkrumah as one of the 'Big Six'

people.name: Nii Kwabena Bonne III
people.role: chief who organised the boycott of European trading firms that filled Accra's streets in the weeks before the shooting

toll.note: The Watson Commission of inquiry recorded 29 dead and 237 injured across the three days. Three of the dead were the ex-servicemen shot at the castle crossroads.

pedagogy.hook: The men Britain arrested for causing the riots of 1948 were governing the country within four years and ruling it within nine.

misconception.belief: Britain planned a gradual, orderly handover of power in Africa.
misconception.correction: In February 1948 the Gold Coast was Britain's model colony and there was no plan to leave. Ex-servicemen were shot on the way to deliver a petition, the towns burned for three days, and within a year Britain had appointed a commission recommending a new constitution. The timetable was set by what happened on the ground, not in London.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: This is the beginning of the end of British Africa, and it started with soldiers who had fought for Britain in Burma asking for the pensions they had been promised.

evidence.author: Dennis Austin
evidence.work: Politics in Ghana, 1946-1960
evidence.supports: The riots, the Watson Commission and the political transformation that followed.

evidence.author: Richard Rathbone
evidence.work: Nkrumah and the Chiefs: The Politics of Chieftaincy in Ghana 1951-60
evidence.supports: The CPP's rise and its conflict with the older political class.

events.title: The British Togoland plebiscite
events.summary: A UN-supervised plebiscite asked British Togoland whether to join the Gold Coast or stay under trusteeship. About 58 per cent chose union; the north voted heavily for it and the Ewe south heavily against.
events.significance: It is the only case of a British territory voting itself out of existence, and the option most Togolanders wanted — reuniting Ewe country across the 1916 border — was never on the ballot.

places.name: Ho
places.note: Centre of Ewe politics in British Togoland.

places.name: Lomé
places.note: Capital of French Togoland, across the line.

people.name: Sylvanus Olympio
people.role: led the Ewe unification campaign and became the first President of independent Togo; assassinated in 1963

people.name: S.G. Antor
people.role: leader of the Togoland Congress, which campaigned against union with the Gold Coast

people.name: Kwame Nkrumah
people.role: campaigned for union and delivered the northern vote

pedagogy.hook: Roughly 93,000 people voted to join Ghana and 67,000 voted not to, and the whole territory joined anyway.

misconception.belief: A referendum settles what people want.
misconception.correction: It settles which of the options on the paper is most popular. The Ewe of southern Togoland wanted their country reunited across the Anglo-French line of 1916, and that was not on the ballot; the choice was union with the Gold Coast or more trusteeship. The result was then applied to the whole territory, including the section that had voted the other way.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Separatist movements in Ghana's Volta region still date their claim from this vote, most recently in the 'Western Togoland' declarations of 2019-20.

evidence.author: D.E.K. Amenumey
evidence.work: The Ewe Unification Movement: A Political History
evidence.supports: The Ewe campaign, the UN petitions and the plebiscite.

contested.note: The exact vote totals are given slightly differently in different sources; the proportion, roughly 58 to 42, and the sharp north-south split are agreed.

events.title: Ghana's independence
events.summary: At midnight in Accra the Gold Coast became Ghana, the first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to take its independence from a European power. Kwame Nkrumah told the crowd that Ghana's independence was meaningless unless linked with the total liberation of Africa.
events.significance: It set the timetable for everyone else. Within nine years more than thirty African colonies had followed, and Accra became the meeting place — the All-African People's Conference of 1958 brought Lumumba, Kenyatta and Nyerere there.

places.name: Accra Polo Ground
places.note: Where Nkrumah declared independence at midnight.

people.name: Kwame Nkrumah
people.role: first Prime Minister and later President; won three elections and a prison term on the way

people.name: Charles Arden-Clarke
people.role: last British governor, who released Nkrumah from prison in 1951 and stayed on as Governor-General

people.name: Baffuor Osei Akoto
people.role: led the Asante federalist opposition that Britain required a third election to settle

pedagogy.hook: Ghana chose 6 March because that was the date in 1844 on which Fante chiefs had signed British jurisdiction into existence.

misconception.belief: Britain handed independence to its African colonies when it judged them ready.
misconception.correction: Britain set the date and drew the constitution; it did not choose whether to go. The Gold Coast had riots in 1948, a general strike in 1950, a leader who won an election from prison in 1951, and three mass elections in six years. Britain conceded when refusing became more expensive than agreeing. 'Granted' is the loser's word for losing.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: Every later African independence is measured against this one. It is also the clearest proof that mass political organisation, not armed struggle, was the commonest route out of the British Empire in Africa.

evidence.author: Dennis Austin
evidence.work: Politics in Ghana, 1946-1960
evidence.supports: The elections, the negotiations and the transfer of power.

evidence.author: Basil Davidson
evidence.work: Black Star: A View of the Life and Times of Kwame Nkrumah
evidence.supports: Nkrumah's politics and pan-African programme.

events.title: Nigeria's independence
events.summary: Nigeria became independent as a federation of three regions under Prime Minister Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, with about 45 million people — more than every other British African territory put together.
events.significance: It removed the largest population Britain ruled in Africa, and it handed over a constitutional structure in which one region held a permanent majority. That structure broke down in the coups of 1966 and the civil war that followed.

places.name: Lagos
places.note: Where the flag was raised at midnight.

people.name: Abubakar Tafawa Balewa
people.role: first Prime Minister

people.name: Nnamdi Azikiwe
people.role: first Nigerian Governor-General and then President

people.name: Obafemi Awolowo
people.role: leader of the opposition; had introduced free primary education in the Western Region in 1955

people.name: Ahmadu Bello
people.role: Premier of the Northern Region and the federation's decisive power broker

pedagogy.hook: One in every three people who left the British Empire in Africa left it on 1 October 1960, in a single country.

misconception.belief: Indian independence in 1947 was the end of the British Empire.
misconception.correction: In 1960 alone Nigeria, Somaliland and Cyprus left, and the next six years took Sierra Leone, Tanganyika, Uganda, Kenya, Zanzibar, Nyasaland, Northern Rhodesia, Gambia, Guyana, Barbados and Botswana. Britain was fighting colonial wars in Malaya, Kenya, Cyprus and Aden in the 1950s. The empire's biggest African losses came thirteen years after India.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The country Britain handed over on this day now holds more people than the whole British Empire in Africa did in 1960, and its constitutional troubles began with the shape of the federation it inherited.

evidence.author: Toyin Falola and Matthew M. Heaton
evidence.work: A History of Nigeria
evidence.supports: The constitutional conferences, the federal settlement and independence.

events.title: The Cameroons plebiscites
events.summary: The two halves of British Cameroons voted on the same day and chose different countries: the north joined Nigeria by roughly 60 to 40, the south joined Cameroon by roughly 70 to 30. Independence was not an option on either ballot.
events.significance: One British territory ended as parts of two states. Cameroon took Britain to the International Court of Justice over the northern result, and the southern result is the origin of the Anglophone conflict that has been fought since 2017.

places.name: Buea
places.note: Capital of Southern Cameroons.

places.name: Foumban
places.note: Where the federal constitution was negotiated in July 1961.

people.name: John Ngu Foncha

pedagogy.hook: One territory voted on one day and split in two: the north woke up Nigerian and the south woke up Cameroonian.

misconception.belief: Decolonisation meant every colony became a country.
misconception.correction: British Cameroons became parts of two other countries. British Somaliland merged into Somalia in 1960. British Togoland joined Ghana in 1957. In each case the ballot or the agreement offered union with a neighbour, not independence. Roughly a tenth of Britain's African territories left the empire by joining somebody else.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: The Anglophone war in Cameroon, which has displaced more than half a million people since 2017, is a direct argument about the choices printed on a ballot paper in 1961.

events.title: The Nigerian civil war and Biafra
events.summary: The Eastern Region declared itself the Republic of Biafra on 30 May 1967 after massacres of Igbo people in the north. Nigeria blockaded and reconquered it in thirty months. Most of the dead were children who starved.
events.significance: The first African war televised into European living rooms. Britain armed the federal side throughout, France armed Biafra, and the images of starving children created modern humanitarian NGOs — Médecins Sans Frontières was founded in 1971 by French doctors who had worked there.

toll.note: The range is enormous because there was no count. Most deaths were from starvation and disease under blockade rather than from fighting, and most of the dead were children. The higher figures come from Biafran and relief-agency estimates, the lower from later demographic reconstructions.

pedagogy.hook: Britain kept supplying the weapons for thirty months while British newspapers ran photographs of the children the blockade was starving.

misconception.belief: Once a colony was independent, the former colonial power's involvement ended.
misconception.correction: Britain was Nigeria's principal arms supplier throughout the war, and it was a deliberate policy: the Foreign Office judged that a united Nigeria protected British oil interests in the delta and British standing in Africa. Independence ended sovereignty over Nigeria; it did not end British interests in it.

pedagogy.whyItMatters: It is the strongest test in this atlas of what colonial legacy actually means. The regional structure that broke down was designed in 1914 and 1954; the oil at stake was found under a colonial concession; and the war was fought with British weapons.

contested.note: The death toll is one of the most disputed figures in modern African history, ranging from about half a million to three million, because no census or count was possible. Historians also disagree about whether the federal blockade amounted to a deliberate policy of starvation.
